speakeroldname: Mr. G. B. NICHOLSON (East Algoma) moved:
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
That the recommendations contained in the second report of the tSpecial Committee appointed for the purpose of inquiring forthwith as to the prices charged throughout Canada for foodstuffs, clothing, fuel, and other neces-

saries of life, etc., presented to the House on Thursday, the 26th day of June, be concurred in. (See Hansard 26th June for this report.)
He said: In moving for the concurrence of the House in this report, I wish to say just a word in regard to the manner in which the report itself was brought in and to the conditions under which it was prepared. In that connection I may say that in reality itr may be looked upon as a minority report, for the reason that the principle involved in the recommendations was only carried by the casting vote of the Chairman of the committee. I may say, further, that subsequent to the passing of the resolution under these circumstances, the validity of the chairman exercising the right of that casting vote was questioned. However, whether the report comes before the House as a minority or as a majority report, those who support the recommendations feel so strongly the desirability of having something done along those lines during this session of Parliament, that they would have been perfectly willing to present the recommendations as a minority report.
Passing to the recommendations contained in the report, the first question that arises is: Is there any necessity for such a tribunal as the recommendations refer to? And that involves two additional questions: First, can such a tribunal as is suggested be of such service to the internal trade o'f this country that it will be to the general advantage of all our people? And, second, have we at present any machinery that can be used for Ithe purposes outlined in the recommendations, and which would avoid the necessity of creating a new tribunal or some additional machinery?
In answer to the first question, I would say without hesitation that there can be no question but that something is required in connection with carrying on the internal trade of the country to satisfy all of the people that they are getting even-handed justice. In the first place, the internal trade of this or any other country is the most important trade that we have, and it cames more closely into the lives of all our people than anything we can possibly have in the nature of external trade. To illustrate that, I will cite just one case, because I want to be exceedingly brief. The question of distribution of foodstuffs, clothing, and all the great variety of commodities that enter into the necessities of life, is of the utmost importance, and we naturally ask what is the best channel through which these commodities can pass from the producer or the manufacturer to

the ultimate consumer. It would be a simple matter to find any number of men who would be ready to tell you at once that our present system is inadequate, that it is cumbersome, that it is too expensive; but it would be an exceedingly difficult matter to find one man who would point to a method or practice that would result in an improvement. But my conviction is that a group of experts, working under the authority of such a tribunal as we have suggested, would very readily get to the bottom of the whole question and point out defects where there are defects, and also point out methods that the people themselves could put into effect to remedy any of these defects and bring about very much more stable and better conditions. It will be conceded that there is nothing so much in the minds of our people as the conviction that profiteering is having a marked effect in enhancing the already abnormal cost of living. For the purpose of this discussion, I shall not express my personal opinion whether these convictions are well founded or not, but the fact that they do exist and that, without question, they are at the bottom of a great deal of the unrest which prevails throughout the country imposes on the Government and on Parliament the immediate responsibility of removing them as far as possible; and my judgment is that nothing will so adequately tend to remove these convictions, to remove from the minds of the people the feeling that they are being unjustly dealt with, as to place at the disposal of the public an independent tribunal to whom all men in all walks of life can appeal whenever and wherever they feel that injustice is being done in a commercial way. The committee that has been inquiring into these subjects has received petitions from all classes of people from all over Canada-consumers, co-operative associations, retail merchants, wholesalers and manufacturers-asking that just such a body as we have recommended be set up in order that all matters pertaining to internal trade may be inquired into and in order that the people may feel that they are getting a square deal.
I would like to cite two specific instances -they might be multiplied to any extent that any one wished to go-in order to emphasize my point. Within the past two or three months there have been two or three sharp rises in the prices of boots and shoes. As far as we have been able to determine, these rises have been due directly to the very great advance in the cost of leather, and this, again, has been brought about by

the fact that a very large part of the available domestic supply has been bought up for export. The balance still remaining has, therefore, been so far enhanced in price that still further advances in the cost of boots and shoes are bound to come unless something is done to bring about a reduction of the cost of leather. Again I say that I am not going to enter into any discussion of the question whether these advances are just or unjust; but if we had such a tribunal as is recommended here, that question could be immediately inquired into, and the public would be in a position to know, without delay, whether or not they were being fleeced. If it was found that they were being fleeced, a remedy could be applied.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: By whom would the remedy be applied, by the Government, or by the tribunal?

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
By the tribunal. The recommendation is that the tribunal shall be independent; at least, that is our understanding of it.
Mr.W. F. MACLEAN: Would that tribunal have power to enforce its own laws, and would it have the machinery to enforce them?

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: That is, without question, involved in the recommendation. The tribunal must be independent and must have within itself the power to make regulations.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: But how about enforcing them?

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: I will give another instance. Evidence was brought to the attention of the committee showing that a woollen product the cost of the manufacture of which in 1914 was $4,374 a dozen was sold to the consumer at $9 a dozen, or 75 cents for each article.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: What kind of wool; where was it from?

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
Canadian wool. The production cost of that article in 1919 was $10.50 a dozen, but the consumer is paying for the article $30 a dozen, or $2.50 for each article, a direct increase of 100 per cent in the spread between the cost of production and the cost to the consumer. These cases might be cited indefinitely, but I have just pointed to two in order to emphasize the point I wish to make; that there is a real necessity for some machinery which will provide that abuses of this kind may be immediately investigated.
I think I speak the mind of most of the men who have been working with me for nearly four weeks on the committee when I say that it took us a very short time to come to the definite conclusion that something else besides a Parliamentary inquiry is necessary. We might keep on forever disclosing these things, but unless something is placed in the hands of some one that will make action possible, these inquiries will do more harm than good, because they simply disclose the condition and create unrest without making any effort to supply a remedy. I cannot conceive oi anything that would be very much worse.
The whole matter is now before the House to be dealt with as the House deems best. My own judgment is that we could do nothing better before the session comes to a close, in an effort to allay the unrest that is sapping the very foundations of our national life, than to make the people feel that there is at their disposal a tribunal of some kind that has the power to act, and will do so. There is no question that the personnel of such a tribunal will determine its value, but our experience with the Railway Board has been of such a nature that we might with a great deal of confidence look forward to the accomplishing of much good in this country by such a board as we have suggested.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at first to a point of order. The report of the committee was voted under very peculiar circumstances. As a matter of fact, the report was voted down by six members of the committee as against five in its favour.
I want to make at first, the declaration that we have the utmost confidence in the integrity and the well-meaning of the Chairman of the committee. He did not mean to do anything which was against the rules; he even took the trouble to inquire from the clerk of the committee what the rule was on the point in question. But his information on the point of order which was raised by members of the committee was bad. He took it for granted that the Chairman of the committee had the right to vote, and had also the right to cast a further vote in the case of there being an equality of vote. I need not deal very extensively with that point. It is well known that the rules of the House in this regard apply to all committees, except, as is provided by Rule 105, in respect of committees on private Bills. The Chairman, therefore, of any committee other than a committee on private Bills has no more right to vote than

the Speaker himself has in the House. But in this case the Chairman of the Committee first voted in favour of the report, and then cast another vote, which made the count seven to six, whereas the actual and legal vote was six to five against the adoption of the report. I submit, therefore, that the report which purports to be the report of the Committee on the Cost of Living is not the report of that committee; and that it should be sent back for further consideration.
But there is something further to be said in this connection. Not only is the report illegal and not only should it be disregarded by the House and sent back to the committee for further consideration, but it is inconsistent in its wording. It says:
Tour committee have been engaged continuously from the &th day of June last to the present date in obtaining all information possible from witnesses and all available sources, but have not yet reached a point in the investigation that would warrant them in submitting final conclusions.
The committee put it clearly that, although they have been engaged from the 5th day of June in hearing evidence, they have not .been able to consider the matter sufficiently to reach final conclusions, and yet the earnestness of the chairman and the minority to put their own conclusions in the shape of a report is such that they insist upon it, and press it through.
To my mind it is premature and will be illusory.
It is premature because we have not studied the matter sufficiently to reach final conclusions, and the machinery suggested to the House will mean an additional and useless expenditure of $200,000 or $300,000 a year.
It is true that there is a great deal of unrest and discontent in the country on account of the huge profits which manufacturers and traders have reaped from the poor labourer, workingman and consumer as a whole. But it is also true that, during the last two or three years, the public at large in Canada are fed with the shields and doors of escape provided by the innumerable Orders in Council and by the no less innumerable commissions created by the present Government. The creation of a new commission will not do away with the cause of the trouble or of the unrest; we must find some adequate remedy, and, to my mind, the proposed commission will not provide it. A few facts will illuminate us in this respect.
There is such .a thing as a Commission on the High Cost of Living already in existence. Doctor McFall was the first

witness heard before the committee, and gave a lengthy evidence on that point. He succeeded Mr. O'Connor who had been appointed by the Government under the Labour Department, just for the purpose of inquiring into the causes influencing the cost of living. Mr. O'Connor, after a full investigation, reached conclusions in 1917, or some two years ago. He laid before the Government a report suggesting the institution of a tribunal or board which should be called the Federal Trade Board or the Federal Trade Commission. If the creation of such a Federal Trade 'Commission was a wise step to take towards reducing the cost of living, why did not the Government act on the report of Mr. O'Connor in 1917? The Government, however, found Mr. O'Connor too inquisitive; his report if adopted would cause trouble to the profiteers; it was not acted upon. Nothing was done except the dismissal of Mr. O'Connor.
The Commission on the Cost of Living continued to exist under the Minister of Labour. Many suggestions were made by the present commissioner, Dr. McFall; none of them was taken into account, and none was made the subject of any legislation brought to this House by the Government. As late as September, 1918, Dr. McFall found out that undue profits were taken by bakers and traders in bread in the city of Halifax. After full investigation he came to a Conclusion in February, 1919, and he at once reported to the Minister of Labour, recommending that legal prosecution be commenced at once. The minister had his report from February to the month of May, but no action was taken. The Minister of Justice has had that report, since May, but he did not move either.

That is a slip of the tongne which happens frequently even with members of the Government. I ask that Hansard correct that error. Of course I meant to say Mackenzie and Mann. And the Bank of Commerce have also reaped quite a harvest of governmental rewards. Another man was also interested in cold storages, and one high up in official circles, and perhaps was he often paralyzed when it was time to act against cold storages, because of his associations. Who is this man? Mr. Shank, the secretary-treasurer of the Manitoba Cold Storage Company, took the trouble to give us the complete list of all the shareholders of that company, and among them we find Mr. Rod. Mackenzie, son of Sir William Mackenzie. We find Sir John Murray's estate; we find a man named Black, connected with the Ogilvie Flour Mills; and we find also Mr. Andrews, manager of the coal mine at Brule Lake, Alberta. But there is another name more prominent in Canadian politics -last, but not the least, we find the name of the Right Honourable Prime Minister of Canada for an investment of nine thousand five hundred dollars. This is a trifling amount to the Prime Minister, and I will not go so far as to say that his interest in this cold storage induced him purposely to adopt certain policies, but it is only human to be influenced by association, and it is only human to want to please friends with whom we are connected in a business enterprise. It is superhuman to do otherwise. I do not believe that a man in public life, much less in the Cabinet, who has to shape the policy of the country, should have any interest in concerns that influence the cost of living.
In view of all that, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the House has only one thing to do and that is to refuse to entertain the report of the committee on the cost of living. The House should return it to the committee for further consideration and, if it dees,
I have no doubt that the committee will come to some other conclusion, which will produce better results than the suggestion now offered to the House. It is not necessary to create special machinery to have action taken before the courts of justice. We have courts of high jurisdiction all over the country. Why should not the Government introduce prosecutions in these courts when

such things are brought to their attention as have been disclosed before this committee, and a long time prior to its selection. If there have been unfair practices against the law of the country which have had the effect of enhancing the cost of living, it seems to me that it was the duty of the Government to bring the offenders before the courts. Such practices have been going, and are going on. The proposed commission will cost $200,000 or $300,000 to the country, but it will hinder the prosecution of the offenders, and fail to produce the desired effect. Therefore, I recommend that the report be sent back to the committee for further consideration.

speechtext:
The facts as stated by the hon. member who has just taken his seat as to the vote in the committee are correct, but I may say that we agreed in the committee that the chairman had two votes. Therefore, in so far as I am able to judge, I will say that the report was in order and absolutely fair. While a discussion arose in the committee as to the chairman having two votes, the bulk of the committee agreed that he had. I would like to point out also that in the committee there was no discussion from a party standpoint. Therefore, I am sorry that the 'hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has introduced party, to a considerable extent, in his argument. His reflections upon the Government and the whole tenor of his remarks in discussing the question this morning have largely tended to throw the onus of responsibility on the
Government. I am glad to say that in the committee there was no such thing as a vote from a party standpoint . Three Unionists and three members of the Opposition voted against the resolution. I would like to make my position perfectly plain this morning. I am not opposed, or was not opposed, to a board of commerce if it is properly constituted. But I am opposed, and have been for the last few years, to the many commissions that have been appointed.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
I know of one or two instances where the commission so appointed did not benefit the country, or benefit anybody, in anything like the proportion of the cost involved to the country by reason of the work of that commission; that is my judgment, although I may be wrong in the view. I know also where a committee asked for the appointment of a commission and recommended that men of outstanding ability, regardless of cost, should be chosen as members of it. Nevertheless, that commission has not given satisfaction to the country since its appointment, although its membership embraces some estimable gentlemen. It is for that reason I speak as I do, not because I do not think a board of commerce might accomplish a great deal of good in investigating commercial questions, especially where a prejudice exists which, in my judgment, is absolutely unfounded, against some corporations; and if a commission did not do any other good it would serve a useful purpose by educating the public as to the exact conditions that surround the cost of living.
Before I forget it, I would like to touch for a moment on what the hon. gentleman has said with respect to the leader of the Government having stock in a certain cold storage company in Winnipeg. Has it come to the point that our public men cannot invest money in any enterprise in this country without being subjected to the suspicion that they are profiteers? If it has, then I hope every respectable man in this country will retire from public life, and let the Government run itself, if such a course is possible. Because if every man who happens to have a little money to invest is debarred from investing it in any industry in Canada, where is he going to get a field for his investments? For everything tends to influence to a certain extent the cost of living, no matter what the nature of his investment may be. Now it was not proved before the committee that there was

anything in the charge that the cold storage corporation in which the Prime Minister has some money invested, was a profiteer; nothing of that character was proved at all. It is a public cold storage where everybody can store their goods, if they so desire, at a certain fixed price, and at a very low price, too, so far as was explained to the committee. Any member of this House, no matter where he resides, could send his eggs, or his butter, or iiis meat, or anything else that he desires, to this cold storage and store it there at a certain fixed price; but no evidence was adduced before the committee to show that there was any unnecessary profit or anything but a reasonable profit, made by the cold storage company in question for the storage of such goods. Therefore, no ground exists for criticism or blame of the Prime Minister, because of his small investment in this particular cold storage plant. A few years ago-doubtless the system is in force to-day-the Government gave a sort of bonus, it engaged in the policy of lending a certain amount of money at a very low rate of interest, for the purpose of encouraging people in Canada to start cold storage plants. That is all I wish to say on that subject.
I would like to point out further that in my judgment there is a very false impression in Canada with respect to large corporations. So far as the investigation before the special committee went to show, it is the large rather than the small corporation that produces more cheaply the goods which enter into consumption among the people, because the former with its splendid organization and its intensive way oi doing business, carries on operations at a very small profit on its turn-
12 noon. over. Whether the profit will be very large on its capital stock or not depends very largely on the amount of that capital stock. If the capital stock is small, the profit on it by reason of the turn-over may he large; if the capital stock is very large the profit will be that much smaller in proportion. But my contention is that the point to ascertain is the amount of toll taken on the turn-over as the goods pass from the original producer through the hands of the corporation or the individual. That is to say, if a man, when the goods pass from the original producer takes a toll of twelve cents, that would represent twelve cents added to the cost of the goods, and he may have made a large profit on his turn-over. Another man, when the goods passes through his hands, may have
	.
added fifty cents to the cost of original production which would represent a large profit on his turn-over, and a small profit on his capital. The whole question, whether it is a corporation or a man that is involved, is as to the amount of toll taken on the goods which pass through the corporation's or person's hands. Let me give an illustration of what I mean. It was clearly proved before the special committee that the packer-that is the concern which is condemned from end to end of this land at the present moment, although I think as the result of a prejudice-got a very small profit on his turn-over but a large profit on his capital, because the latter was very small in comparison with the former. Take, for example, the Harris abattoir. They proved that they could supply beef cheaper to the butcher than he could go out and buy beeff for in competition with them; they realized one-quarter of one per cent on their turryrver, or twenty-five cents on the hundred, and still they made a large profit on their capital; they had a turnover of something like $38,000,000 on a capital of about $1,500,000. That will illustrate exactly the point I am trying to make. Take the Grain Growers' Corporation, a marvellously well-conduetedi and systematically managed organization. Well, that organization did not put their money into a good deal of the business they turned over. That business was on consignment, and they did not actually invest their money in it. They had a turnover of $102,000,000 in 1917, if I remember correctly, and they made a profit of -44, less than one-half of one per cent. Still, it was a good profit on their capital and was due to the business being so capably managed. Then take the Harris abattoir. They made a profit of -25, or one-quarter of one per cent, as against a profit by the Canadian Grain Growers' Association of -44, or a little less than one-half per cent. Nevertheless, the Harris abattoir are condemned as profiteers when they are not. It is the same way with the celebrated Davis Company. My hon. friend has thrown out a slur against Sir Joseph Flavelle, and we have heard an awful lot of the same kind of talk in this House. Mr. O'Connor's report in regard to that concern shows that if it had not been for the enormous turn-over of forty-five or forty-eight million dollars, with the very small profit on their turn-over, they would not have realized any return on their capital. But Sir Joseph Flavelle's company, the Davis Company, showed us most clearly that with their chain of retail stores they

only made a profit of two and a half per cent on their turn-over, and everybody who is familiar with those stores knows that they sell their meats just as cheaply, if not more so, than the local butcher. Now that company cannot be blamed for the profit they made. It was owing ito their expert organization, and their intensive business methods, that they were able to make a profit on their turn-over of two <and a half per cent, although that undoubtedly is a large profit on their capitalization. But if they had wiped out one-half per cent on the whole of the company's business, it would not have taken much to convert their profit into a loss, and a corporation that does business on so close a margin deserves a lot of credit, in my judgment, for producing goods at the lowest possible cost to the consumer. And that was what we were there to investigate.
A great deal of notice was given in the newspapers to Mr. Paton, who made 72 per cent on his capital. But it must be borne in mind that that man had been in business for forty-eight years, I think, for fifteen of which he never paid a cent to his shareholders. He had accumulated a reserve of $644,000, and in speaking of the profit on the capital of $600,000, no credit was given to him for that reserve, which was nothing else but capital-accumulated out of his profits, quite true, but at the same time accumulated because of careful management and by not paying dividends to his shareholders, which he might quite proparly have distributed. Now, as a matter of fact, he made a profit on his turn-over of 12 per cent in 1916, of 11 per cent in 1917, and of 13 per cent in 1918. In other words, goods that cost him $1 in 1916 he turned out to the public at $1.12; goods that cost him $1 in 1917*he turned out to the public at $1.11; and goods that cost him $1 in 1918 he turned out to the public at $1.13. I freely own that owing to the amount of business he was doing he was extracting too much profit. He could have safely done business at a less profit. At the same time it must be borne in mind that he was doing business on a very reasonable profit had he only a small turn-over, but his turn-over was very large during these years, owing to the fact that he was making cloth for the countries that were at war, and was: running night and day on one particular grade of cloth, which enabled him to make a much larger profit than he could have done had he been obliged to change his machine every few hours, as would be the case in the ordinary
course of business. I am not pretending to defend anything that may be an overprofit, but I am saying that in my judgment regard should not be had to the amount of profit made on the capital, but to the amount of toll taken by the individual or the corporation between the time of the production of the goods until they eventually reached the retailer.
We found that in a place like Ottawa when it comes t-o the retailer-and I would like to emphasize this-that on account of his enormous expense for rent, taxes and one thing and another, he has to have a very wide spread between his purchase price and 'his sale price, and I think in many instances he is taking a toll from the consumer that is absolutely unnecessary. There are so many people anxious to jump into the retail trade that in one block you will have four or five stores doing the same 'kind of business, and because their turn-over is small and their expenses are heavy they have to charge too much to the consumer to get a profit. That is one of the things we found. I am only speaking of my own view in these matters.
Now, as to a Board of Commerce. If I was sure that the Government would appoint men of outstanding ability, men who thoroughly understood the necessities of business in this country, I would be in favour of such a board; but I would rather discuss that when the Bill for its appointment comes before the House, because I would like to know what powers it is proposed to give such a board. The Federal Trade Commission are given an investigatory power. My experience has been that if a commercial question is investigated and the facts published fairly, that their publication alone will right anything wrong. How would you give a Board of Commerce the right to fix prices? You might give it that right as between the producer and the consumer, but you could not possibly give it that right as to the producer alone, because the cost of production varies every day. Take the cost of production from the farm. If a man can raise forty bushels of wheat to the acre instead of only ten bushels, the cost of production will be very different, and unless you can get the powers above to tell you what crop is going to be given the farmers, I do not see how you are going to regulate the cost of wheat, nor the cost of other grains, which cost depends absolutely on production. We can estimate easily enough what it would cost to produce wheat if the average crop was twenty-

. five, twenty or fifteen bushels to the acre, but we cannot tell what it is going to be.
Now, as to manufactures, there is no board of commerce that can set the price at which a manufacturer shall sell his goods from week to week. It is absolutely impossible to do justice in that regard, because it depends on the cost of labour, and the cost of raw material. How is any board of commerce going to set the cost of raw material? It may be bought in Canada, but it may be bought in all parts of the world. We all know that in large manufacturing industries they import goods from every part of the world where they can get them the cheapest. Therefore you have got to stop regulating when you come to the producer either of the manufactured article or of the foodstuffs of the country. So that I would not be in favour of a board of commerce that had the right of regulation. I am not opposed to a board of commerce constituted of the right type of men who would investigate all questions where there was dissatisfaction and where there was a tendency to what is called combination. There is a vast difference between a combination and a large organization as the result of a merger. A combination is a unity between different corporations of the same kind to fix the price of goods.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that this report, which is a minority report, is declared: to be in order, the question that is really before the House is the apparent decision of the Government to appoint another commission. But I wish to point out that the conditions of which we are complaining are conditions which have been created under commissions; we have had commissions and control boards throughout the country until the people are tired of them.
It was pointed out to the Parliament of that day when the Federal Food Control Board was appointed that food control would not only be a failure; but would be a heavy tax upon the people. I have before me the report of the debate on the occasion of the presentation to the House of the first report of the Food Board, when it was represented to us that the cost to the country of the operations of this Board would not be more than $150,000 a year. We on this side contended that the cost would run up to over $400,000 a year, and as a matter of fact the figures given by the Food Board itself show that the cost to the country was something over $500,000 a year, or, to be more exact, $491,968 for a period of eleven months. Who bears that expense, Mr. Speaker? The people of the country. The Food Board issued licenses to dealers throughout the country-to the baker, the butcher, and the grocer, and the baker, the butcher, and the grocer passed along to the people the cost of those licenses, with 100 per cent profit. So that it is the people, after all, who bear this enormous expense. Price-fixing has been a failure in Canada; France discovered early in the game that it was a failure. Tn my judgment, the real remedy is competition. After all, the good old rule that competition is the life of trade still holds good.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: In giving the cost of the Food Board, did the hon. gentleman deduct the fees collected by the board in respect of these licenses?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
That is exactly the point 1 am making; it is the people who are paying for this. The fees collected amount to $366,261. Who paid those fees? As I pointed out in opening, they were paid by the consumer, with 100 per cent profit added; the payment of these fees was only an excuse for the dealers throughout the country to pass them along to the consumer with a

profit. Not only was this the case, but competition was destroyed. Many people went out of business; they said: We are not going to bother with all these regulations; and the fellows who were doing business and paying fees to the Food Board were jacking up prices to the people.
There is nothing in the report of this committee to show what percentage of these enormous profits were made out of the people of Canada. It is quite possible that a large percentage of these profits were made out of foreigners, and I submit that it is not going to hurt this country if Canada makes profits out of foreigners. If the industries of Canada make big profits, no matter how big, out of foreigners and foreign trade, this country is not injured. The more profits the industries of this country can make, the better it is for the country and the better for the Finance Minister, who taxes the surplus profits.
I wish to point out to the Prime Minister and to the Chairman of this committee that we now have in the legislation of this country, under section 12 of the Customs Tariff of 1907, all the power that is required to deal with combines that are unduly restraining trade. Section 12 is as follows:
Whenever, from or as a result of a judgment of the Supreme Court or Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any superior court, or circuit, district or county court in Canada it appears to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that with regard to any article of commerce there exists any conspiracy, combination, agreement or arrangement of any kind among manufacturers of such articles or dealers therein to unduly promote the advantage of the manufacturers or dealers at the expense of the consumers, the Governor in Council may admit the article free of duty, or so reduce the duty thereon as to give the public the benefit of reasonable competition in the article, if it appears to the Governor in Council that such disadvantage to the consumer is facilitated by the duties of customs imposed on a like article.
The Government, therefore, have all the *legislative authority that (they require. During all the years that this tariff was administered by the Liberal administration, there was no complaint of the high cost of living. There was a complaint of the high cost of paper at one time, and the Finance Minister of that day, the present-member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), called these gentlemen in and said: "If you do not- bring your prices down to a reasonable basis, I will take advantage of this clause"; and they climbed down, because they knew that a Government was in power that meant business. Instead of appointing more commissions that will impose additional burdens upon
274	'
the people, that will hamper trade and reduce competition, I suggest that the Government get down to business and take advantage of the clause in the tariff which enables them to control these trusts and combines. It does not make any difference what the cost of living is in Canada, so long as it is no higher than it is in neighbouring countries; that is the real issue. If we sell our goods at home at prices no higher than those at which we sell them abroad, there is no reasonable cause for complaint. If the western farmer sells his wheat in Canada at the same price as that which he obtains overseas, nobody has any fault to find; and so it should be with all the trade of the country. If the Government are of the opinion that there are combines which are unduly advancing the prices of the necessaries of life, they have a remedy in the customs tariff.	'

speakeroldname: Mr. FRANCIS HENRY KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as reference has been made particularly to the Food Board, I feel it my duty to say something in this debate, because I was connected with the work of that board. The hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) claims that too much money was taken out of the people by the Food Board, and he



also voices his complaint as against the institution of a Food Board, that it would cost money. The inference is that no matter what was done, it would be all wrong. As a matter of fact, the Food Board paid its own expenses for the entire time it was in operation, and in addition, it handed in to the treasury of Canada $39,000 at the and of its operations. It is these misleading *statements at this time of unrest that, perhaps unintentionally, are causing a great deal of additional unrest, and what the country wants is correct information disseminated. For instance, the hon. member for Lotbinifere (Mr. Vien) gave the impression to this House, and thereby to the whole country, that the Prime Minister was a profiteer because he had some money invested in a cold storage plant. I understand from what the hon. member for Oxford North (Mr. Nesbitt) said that it developed in the committee perfectly clearly that that company was dealing only in cold storage warehousing, and that it was not buying nor selling the products. If so, is it fair for an hon. member to endeavour to create such an impression? Is it not the policy of this House to-day to advocate the building oi these cold storage warehouses throughout the country and to assist the municipalities if they will build them? And because a man, in the meantime, prior to that being done, has been forwarding that movement, is it not rather unfair to make an innuendo in the House about the matter?
But I pass on. * What we ought to endeavour to do is to get at the causes of these high prices and to try to remedy them. The Prime Minister, since his return, has very ably pointed out the effect of a large number of men being taken from production and put into destructive work such as war. We all know that, practically at any ordinary time during the year, the world has never more than sixty days' supplies ahead, and if you take away from productive work a large number of men, you naturally decrease the production, and we very soon have the demand exceeding the supply. But to my mind, arising out of and in addition to that, the great cause of our difficulty to-day and what we ought to endeavour to remedy if we possibly can is the competitive buying of the world in our markets. The Hon. W. J. Hanna was appointed some two years ago as food controller, and the hon. member for Lot-binifere (Mr. Vien) must have forgotten that when he stated that nothing was done and when he asked:	Why was not something done two years ago? Mr. Hanna was

appointed, and a new organization created to endeavour to grapple with that problem and in my opinion it did exceedingly well. The cry against Mr. Hanna in all parts of the country at that time was: Why do you not fix prices? Fortunately he was not stampeded; he knew too well from his business knowledge that price fixation is the greatest fallacy and he steered clear of it. The only price fixation we have in this country was first the price of wheat fixed by the Wheat Export Company, not by the Food (Board, at $2.20 a bushel, and second, arising out of that, the price of bran and shorts was fixed, f.o.b., Fort William. But what was done by the Food Board after it got its hand on the throttle was to fix the spread, and the spread of the wholesaler and that of the dealers were fixed, and that so far as the domestic market is concerned, was a wise policy to pursue, you cannot go in for price fixation; the matter of buying and selling is as old as the hills and if you attempt to fix prices, you get into difficulties because price takes the place of the old barter and exchange, you must fix price of everything, you must fix the price of labour and that means compulsory labour. But you can regulate the spread.
When the Food Controller was appointed, his primary object was to see that as pauch food as possible was sent overseas, and his secondary object was to control and regulate the trade of the country within its boundaries.
That the Food Board has fairly well succeeded in the primary object of getting food exported to our Allies appears from the 13th page of its report, which shows that the value of the exports of foodstuffs in 1914-15 was $187,000,000, whereas the value in 191718 was $710,000,000, or about four times as much. Therefore, the primary object was fulfilled. Then it grappled with the secondary object, namely, the regulations. The first thing it had to do was to get at the cause of the jumping up of prices in Canada, and it was quickly realized that this was due to the competitive bidding and buying of the Allies. Finally the Allied Purchasing Committee was created and it took control of the allied buying, with result that you did not have Italy competing against France for cheese and France competing against England for condensed milk, but all bought through the one Allied Purchasing Committee. With that there was enacted the hoarding order, which prevented unnecessary hoarding in the country. Returns were made with the result that any

unnecessary surplus stocks in the country were ordered to be sold, and there was only one source outside of the country to buy and they, the Allied Purchasing Commission, had a tacit arrangement with the Food Board that they would not offer a higher price than the local prices. The result was that in that way prices were somewhat controlled. Then came the armistice, with the result that that arrangement ceased, and to-day we have in addition all the neutral countries of the world in the markets here, starved heretofore, paying any price to get what they want, and prices are rising, and in my judgment we shall have prices rising further yet; especially when peace comes, when we shall have the enemy countries coming into the market and also competing for our goods, It seems to me that apart from the regulation of the spread or profit, not the turnover, we cannot regulate this question of food prices until some definite arrangement is worked out by which international buying and competition is under control.
When that is done probably the prices will steady themselves and in time the production will catch up to the demand and prices come back somewhat to normal. It is our duty as members of this House to endeavour to grapple with the true cause in this matter and apply the remedy. There are several causes for this rise in price, among them the increased amount of circulation in the country which is double now what it was before. There was a pile of goods as against a pile of money and the dollar had its purchasing value, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Brome in the Budget debate; and as he frankly admitted the circulation reasonably had, to be increased through the necessities of the war. We then had double the pile of money to spend on the former pile of goods and th'e dollar consequently had half its purchasing value. At the present time, we should not make misleading statements to the country.
We are going through a very crucial period in Canada, a period to my mind equally as crucial as that which menaced us at the time of the German forward movement early in 1918. There is unrest all over Canada as well as throughout the whole world, and it is the duty of every one of us to try as far as possible to allay the trouble here by being at least careful to see that any information we give to the country is accurate and reliable. We members are going home to our constituencies and we should make it a point to take with
274}
us such facts as will enable us to discuss properly and intelligently the real cause of these high prices. Is it the tariff? The Food Board report issued under the hand of the hon. ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) shows that in September of last year, when the Food Board practically ceased business, the prices of staple commodities in Canada were ten per cent lower than they were, in the United States. I need not take up the time of the House enlarging on this point. As the hon. member for Oxford has shown, the prices are lower here, and the tariff is therefore not a factor, at the present time at all events. Profiteering is not a factor either. The profits that men are making to-day in this country are due to the large volume oi business done overseas, the spread or extent to which they are profiting out of the-consumers in the country is no greater than it used to be. If, however, we find that on any particular article there is too-much spread, then the commission or any body which it is contemplated to appoint can deal with the matter. I would say just a word or two on the question of commissions.
It has been very fashionable in the last year or two to slam, in every possible way, every commission. A rose will be absolutely the same no matter how you designate it. We have commissions that are not slammed, such as the Railway Commission. But the doctrine that is generally preached is that commissions are irresponsible bodies not under the control of this House. There are two answers to that: First, they are under the control of this House, being always under some minister. The food controller, for instance, was under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture. In the next place, we went through a time of stress when the /Civil (Service had three to four times the volume of business to do and they were simply worked to death, and men came in like the Hon. Mr. Hanna to give to the country without remuneration the best services they could until they found they could stand it no longer and resigned. It is rather ungrateful that no recognition is taken of that class of service. In my judgment, no man, through the critical time that this country experienced, rendered greater service than the Hon. Mr. Hanna, who was grappling with a difficult problem, an untried matter, and had the courage to stick to it, ignoring popular abuse and refusing to be stampeded. If any one will take the trouble to read the report issued by the board, he must come to the conclusion, if he'is reasonable, that

the work of the commission has been, well worthy of commendation instead of abuse. I do not know what the policy is as regards this particular Act which is coming forward, but if we desire to regulate prices and control them we must do two things. We will have to control the international buying and keep control of the exportation for a year or so until times right themselves. During the Food Board days it was found necessary to control all exports going out of the country so that they could, not reach the neutrals. The result was that the Allied Commission could buy freely, but no one else could export, the object being that *exports should be kept from going to enemy *countries. Some principle such as that could be worked out in this matter of regulating food for the next two years. The export business should be conducted by permit so as not to have too much going out with resultant shortage and famine prices. We must bear in mind, however, that there are starving countries to-day competing in our markets for our products, both food and manufactured goods, and we cannot interfere with that in such a way as to shut ourselves in and take the ground that none of our products will go out. We must pay our debts, and a good way to do it is to export our goods, agricultural and manufactured, and at the same time endeavour to regulate international demand . and thus control somewhat the rising prices at this critical period. .

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: We are faced with a proposition in regard to procedure to which I wish to refer. It is very well to say that you, Sir, or any other court must recognize a document as being regular if it is regular on its face. But when it is brought to the notice of a court by competent evidence that although ,a document which appears on its face to he regular is in reality irregular, the court will no longer regard that document as being worthy of credence. Suppose a man goes into court with a deed of a piece of land appearing on the face of it to be perfectly regular, purporting to be signed by the vendor, properly witnessed, duly sworn to and recorded. The court in the first instance will presume that it is a regular document; but the moment it is proven to the satisfaction of the court that the vendor did not sign the document at all, of course it is no longer valid and will fall to the ground.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: Order. Do I understand that the hen. gentleman is calling into question the decision of the Chair?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: No. I am dealing with the question of procedure. We are establishing a precedent, that the minority of a committee can report to this House and that we have no remedy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: My decision was in exact conformity with the well established practice which has heretofore obtained in this House and in the British House of Commons, and in conformity with the exact letter and spirit of the rules. The procedure is well recognized, but in any event, if any question is to be raised, this can only be done by way of appeal at the time the decision is rendered. It is competent for this House to refer back to a Committee for its consideration a report with or without instructions. It would then be competent for the Committee to deal with that question and make a report to the House to determine as to the validity of any given proceeding, exception to which had been taken in the Committee and a report thereon presented to the House. But as the report now before us is complete in form and regular, it is not competent for the House to call into question the regularity of the proceedings of the Committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: I have an authority on the question. It is the rule of the Lords that in Committee the Chairman votes like any other peer, and if the members be equal on division the question is negatived. That is the rule. It is the rule of the English Commons, that the Chairman of a select committee can only vote when there is an equality of voices. The practice of the English House prevails in the Senate and Commons of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
The hon. member, I
think, misapprehended the point altogether.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: No, I did not.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: My decision had no reference whatever to the legality of the proceedings in the committee; it was simply that it was not competent to raise that question in the House under the circumstances.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: Perhaps the Speaker can direct us how it can be raised, but there is an irregularity before this House and are we to be bound by that irregularity and is there to be no remedy? If I were in the Supreme Court I would have a remedy at once because if an irregular document were offered and objection raised it could not be acted upon; otherwise, it could not be a properly constituted court.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member that it is competent for this House to refer the report back to the committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: I understood that there was a motion to that effect made. However, if it is competent for me to do so I shall move that the report be not confirmed but that it be referred back to the committee for further consideration. I may not have another opportunity of saying that I do not approve of creating any further machinery to deal witlh these matters. Already we have eighteen or twenty departments of government. We have the Departments of Trade and Commerce, Justice, and Labour that come closely to this subject matter and if another official or two is necessary to be appointed to any of these departments to enable them to deal with this question, I would be in favour of such appointment. But I am not in favour of creating a new, raw, court that knows nothing whatever about these matters to start experimenting for the next five or six years at enormous expense to the country. Surely we have in the Department of Trade and Commerce, which has existed for the last fifteen years enough experience that can be utilized for the purpose of carrying out anything that is necessary to be done to relieve the situation. Surely we have in the Department of Labour, which is at least twelve or fifteen years old, sufficient experience, supplemented by an expert or two, to carry out its duty. If the Combines Act, or any other Act, either criminal or civil, which should be brought into play to punish the profiteer is not sufficient at the present time, let us legislate and make it sufficient to enable the department to punish the man who is unduly profiteering in carrying on his business in this country.

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: Who would enforce that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
I would certainly enforce the law, and enforce it to the limit, against any person who is unduly profiteering and sucking the lifeblood out of the poor people of this country. I would do that without any hesitation whatever. 1 think it should have been done long ago, and if the chairman of this committee (Mr. Nicholson), in his speech this morning has truly represented to this House the evidence that has been brought before the committee, it should certainly have been done long ago. It is pointed out to us by the Government as a matter of pride that they have taken
part of these undue profits. They say: We have done something; we have caught this thief as he was running away, and we have taken some of the loot from him. Did they return it to the poor man from whom it was taken? No, they kept it, put it in their own pockets, and _this country is profiting by that money. The millionaires are profiting by the undue profit that they have taken out of the pocket of the poor man who has to earn his living at the face of the coal mine, or in the lumber camps, or in the other labouring centres. Is it an answer to the man who cannot get beef, or meat or flour, or bread for his children, to say: True, the profiteer has made $80,000,000 or $100,000,000 out of you, but when he was running away with it we caught him and we took some of it from him. If a man has $20 stolen out of his house or out of his pocket and the policeman says: I caught that man with the $20, I took $5 out of the $20 from him, and he went away with the $15, and I am going to keep $5 myself, is that any remedy for the man who loses his $20?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext: Would it be a remedy ii the money was returned to the purchaser as was done by the Food Board in several cases?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
We know nothing about any private knowledge that any private member may have. We have been questioning the Government, and the only answer we get is that they have taken some of the profits. I submit that that is not a remedy at all, and that it is simply in line with the illustration that I have given of a man whose money is stolen and some officer prides himself on having taken some of the money from the thief and on having kept it himself rather than return it to the owner. The only suggestion of a policy which we have received from the Government is that they should take some of the profits. What the people of this country want is not that a portion of these extraordinary profits should be taken, but that if possible things should be so regulated that goods are sold at a reasonable price so that the ordinary individual can manage to get enough food to eat and enough clothing to wear for himself and his children during this critical period through which we are passing.
There are many things that might be said upon this subject but there is just one that I want to point out. We have this report from the Nicholson committee, as I choose

to call it. We have another report from the Industrial Relations Commission. Both of them happened to come to us this morning. There has been no opportunity of knowing very much about what is in either of them. They may be dealing with the same thing or they may be dealing with different things; they are certainly dealing with the same subject. I would suggest that when the report that we are dealing with now in the House is sent back to the committee,	report	of this	IndustrialRelations Commission should be sent back also and let them try to extract from both a concurrence of opinion and see what is to be done. I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is most anomalous that we should have	two	reports	dealing	practicallywith	the	same	subject.	We havean idea of what is in one of these reports but as to the other we know absolutely nothing about it. It is a document which	does	not come before	the House
under a formal motion and the rank and file know nothing about it. I think it is very desirable that there should be no conflict of opinion as between these two reports, that something should be done to reconcile them if reconciliation is necessary and that the report finally submitted to this House should embody the concurrence of opinion as presented by both. There will be no power on the part of the committee to vary the report of the Industrial Relations Commission hut there may be something in that report that will modify the report of the committee. I do not think there should be two reports one of them possibly saying one thing and the other saying the exact contrary and both advising the same Government.
It is none of my business, Mr. Speaker, but I think it would be advisable that the Government should have the combined wisdom of these two bodies in one report, ii that could possibly he accomplished. In order to proceed regularly I therefore move:

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am a member of the committee whose report is now under consideration. Unfortunately, however, I was not able to give as close attention 
to its meetings as I desired, owing to various causes, and particularly owing to my desire to be present at the sessions of the House, which for some time have been held morning, afternoon and night. It is my desire to pay all due resipect and deference to the conclusions reached by the gentlemen who were able to give more regular attention to the matter than I myself was able to give to it. I know that the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson.) and the vicechairman the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and three or four other members in particular, whom I might designate, have given very patient attendance day by day to the work of the committee, and I know they all approached the question with a sincere desire to have a thorough and effective investigation.
I think the report of tihe committee is regularly before the House; but I think the information that has been given concerning the circumstances under which the report was prepared is abundantly sufficient to justify the motion that that report should be referred back for further consideration. It may be that the House and the Government ara prepared to take up the contemplated legislation, irrespective of any committee report. If that be the case, then what I am about to say, perhaps, is not to the point. But this I may fairly say, that if it is in contemplation to bring forward legislation to be fortified by this committee's report, then surely we ought to have a report of a more valuable character than that which has been presented to us. When I say a report of a more valuable character, I mean a stronger report. A report brought in to the House by a majority at a small meeting, irrespective of the fact that it was by the casting vote of the chairman, certainly is hardly a sufficient ground upon which to undertake grave and important legislation. I therefore think that the argument in favour of referring the matter back to the committee is strong and conclusive and I shall vote for the motion to that effect.
Let me frankly say, however, that in doing so I have no anticipation that if the matter is referred back, the committee will be able to accomplish anything important during the present session. The difficulty is that the job which the committee undertook was too big. It would have been a big job if it had been begun in the earlier stages of the session; but begun at a later stage, when the session was pretty well advanced, it

was beyond possibility that the committee could make any very effective investigation. The scope assigned to the committee was too broad, the questions were too big, the time given for inquiry was too short to justify the expectation that much could be done. I myself formed at an early stage of the meetings of the committee the impression that all we could hope to accomplish at the present stage would be in the way of publicity, and in that respect I think much good has already been done, and I have no doubt that in the further meetings hon. gentlemen contemplate holding any further publicity will serve a good purpose in that respect; but beyond that I have no expectation that anything effective can be done now.
It appears to me, Sir, that the legislation which the committee are advising, and -which it is assumed the Government will take up, is too broad and too important to be put through this House at the present session. I know the argument that is used: Something must be done. That is the whole story. There is a deep feeling of discontent owing to the high cost of living, and the universal cry is: Something must be done. My observation is that in nine cases out of ten the man who demands that something should be done has not the faintest ccn-cept'on of what that something is. And that is the case before us now. I frankly say that it is not easy to determine what- is the something that Parliament at this stage migh do to meet the difficulty.
It seems to me that the Bill which is proposed and recommended in general terms by this committee must of necessity be one of the most important measures of the session. I do not know of any tribunal the creation of which is likely to give us more difficulty than the one which is contemplated in this report. There is more difficulty in defining the powers and authority of a tribunal such as is proposed than there would be in defining the jurisdiction of a new supreme court. There are a thousand difficulties in the way. It is a very, very difficult question to determine, and I am satisfied that if we were to get it through even this House, it is a physical impossibility that in the few days that are left to us now that a Bill of this character can be carried through the two Houses of the legislature. Feeling, therefore, that that is ' not likely to be accomplished, I frankly say that I think the wiser course would be for the Government to let the matter stand for the present and take more time for further consideration, in order to endeavour
to frame a Bill and bring it before us at a time which will give us a better opportunity for considering it. It seems to me that any effort we make now will of necessity be' a hurried effort, and that we will not reach a thoroughly satisfactory conclusion.
Holding these views, Sir, I shall vote to refer the matter back to the Committee, and I shall do so because I believe that we can accomplish nothing very satisfactory during the present session. I quite appreciate the widespread desire that something shall be done. In passing a measure such as is proposed now in a hurried way there will be the appearance of doing something, and possibly for a few days there may seem to be a concession to that demand on the part of public opinion, but a little later I am persuaded the conclusion will be reached that nothing has been done of an effective character. The Committee do not contemplate, I understand, to recommend the regulation of prices. I am not an advocate for the fixing of prices, but I know that in the public mind any measure which falls short of fixing prices will be disappointing, and that is one respect in which .1 think the legislation will fail to accomplish the purpose it has in view.
I am not saying this by way of criticism of what has occurred, but there is a feeling that we have too many commissions and committees and tribunals dealing with these things, and I am afraid public opinion will not view with favour the creation in a hurried way of another tribunal which will land us into enormous expense and in all probability will fail to accomplish the purpose we have in view.

speechtext:
I dislike to project myself into the debate at this time, but I shall only keep the House a moment or two. I always listen with great pleasure to the remarks of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens because they are generally wise and thoughtful, but in this case I believe his recommendations favouring delay would be absolutely fatal. I spent eight or ten days in the West quite recently, and I was so impressed with the universal feeling of indignation there against profiteering that I took the liberty of wiring.the Government that something ought to be done at once to either correct the evil or make a vigorous effort to do so. As a matter of fact the country is aflame with anger over profiteering, and the revelations before the special committee on the High Cost of Liv-

ing have only served to accentuate that anger. People see reports in the press that profiteering exists anywhere from ten and twenty-five per cent up to three hundred per cent, and the result has had an intensely irritating effect upon the people, and if we were to adjourn without making some honest effort to control and correct the situation, I 'believe that a great mistake would be made.
I have a great deal of sympathy with the position the Government took at the outset, that competition and supply and demand, as my hon. friend from Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Eobb) remarked this morning, and the tariff might regulate the situation. But it is my deliberate judgment, based upon what I saw myself, and what I heard on all hands that that will not do. We might adjourn and do nothing, but if we did so I believe we would probably cause very much greater unrest-indeed, it would be accentuated to the degree possibly of revolution. Behind the great strike in Winnipeg there was undoubtedly an element that wanted to set up' a Soviet Government, and it was surprising to me what a great number of the people sympathized with the idea of such a change, not only in Winnipeg, but in other parts of Canada. To a great extent that sentiment was due to the fact that the people are dissatisfied, they believe that the rich are growing richer, and that the poor are growing poorer. They see dividends paid on millions and millions of watered stock, they see interlocking combinations and high finance, and they have a pretty shrewd idea, that something is radically wrong; and unless their representatives undertake to correct that evil, I would not like to be accountable for the consequences.
After all, the duty rests on the Govern

ment-the Opposition will not be blamed- and I believe this Government is bound either to attempt to regulate this malignant state of affairs or to demonstrate that it cannot be regulated. I know and sympathize entirely with the view of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens about the enormous number of commissions that have been appointed from time to time, and the indifferent results obtained from some of them, and I want to say to the Government at once that if the Board of Commerce, which it is proposed to appoint to deal with the present issue which approaches a crisis, is to be in character and composition anything like many of the commissions that have been appointed in the past, it will be just as well to "can"
[Mr. Richardson. 1
the project right now. Unless we have the right kind of men to participate in this very important wbrk it would be better that no Board of Commerce should be appointed. I think in order to make such a board effective, the consumers ought to have the opportunity of nominating a representative *-and I would say that we ought to avoid the appointment of lawyers.. We have too many lawyers on these boards, they tangle up the situation with a mass of legal verbiage and the people get no results. Let us have no lawyers on these commissions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say, in respect to what my hon. friend from the West (Mr. JULY 1, 1919
Richardson) has advanced, that I had not considered myself at liberty to engage in that line of discussion, because, as the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) have pointed out, what is really before us is the reception of this report. I should like to say further in regard to what my hon. friend has advanced, that whether we receive the report or refer it back to the committee does not necessarily have the slightest bearing upon the action of the Government in regard to the very alarming state of affairs which my hon. friend has described. If that be the state of affairs in Western Canada and my hon. friend gave the information at his disposal to the Government by telegram before he delivered the very alarming speech to which we have just listened, the Government have a very obvious duty apart altogether from this report, and that is to proceed to take some steps to deal with the serious situation on their own responsibility. I take it, therefore, that we may approach the only matter that is really before the House at this time without feeling that any action we take has any bearing whatsoever upon the Government's proposed legislation-for I suppose we are right in assuming that the Government purposes legislating after we have dealt with this report in one way or another. I shall reserve anything I have to say, if I have anything to say at all, with regard to the unrest and the cost of living and the other questions which will naturally arise on that legislation, until the legislation itself is before the House.
I have been thoroughly at one with what has fallen from my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) and the leader of the Opposition in regard to this report. I should not question for a moment the Speaker's ruling this morning, even if I thought the ruling was not right; but I was thoroughly satisfied that the ruling was right and that, technically, and abstractly, the report is properly before us. But we cannot shut our eyes to the fact of how it is before us. Two members of this House announced to the whole House that the report was a report of a minority of the committee and so far as I know, they were not contradicted. So that what we are asked to do is to receive a report of a minority, to receive the report of a committee which was carried in point of fact and in reality by a minority of that committee. My mind is so constituted that I cannot subscribe to that course of action and I shall vote against the reception of the report and for its being referred back to
the committee for further consideration-I should do so on that ground alone. Of course, it is perfectly obvious that the report is the result of an S.O.S. call from the Government-no doubt can enter any one's mind about that fact-and if the majority wants to adopt a minority report as the report of a whole committee, as they probably will, of course the report will be adopted and we shall judge the legislation based upon it when it comes before us.
The proceeding of appointing the committee which has reported, was an exceedingly hurried proceeding, undertaken in the last weeks of the session, or what were expected to be the last weeks of the session; and the presentation of the report is, if possible, a more hurried proceeding than the appointment of the committee and the sittings of the committee-I say this upon the evidence which we have had here this morning.
I addressed, Mr. Speaker, to my hon. friend on your left (Mr. Vien) a question as to what the committee had done in regard to investigating the machinery which already exists under the law for the very purpose for which legislation, I understand, is now to be introduced-the investigation of combines. I cannot agree with the member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) when he said this morning that there were some complaints as to the conditions of society or as to the high cost of living at the time that legislation was undertaken, because that legislation was undertaken on account of the tremendous outcry there was in this country at that time about combines. That legislation was meant to meet a public outcry; it was brought in for that purpose. However, I am not concerned with that now; what I am concerned with is that a member of the committee informs us that the subject which would appear to me. most vital to their consideration and deliberation they were unable to handle because they had not time. That is to say; the work of the committee in drawing this report was so hurried that, on. their own evidence, they could not draw up a proper report; they could not draw up a report based upon as 'thorough an examination as the majority of the members of that committee would like to have made. My hon. friend assents to my proposition. On these grounds I could not respect my intellect if I reported for the reception of this report. For what is it that it recommends to us? It recommends to us fresh machinery to deal with certain evils in the body politic, although the committee have not had time to examine into the

effectiveness or ineffectiveness of the machinery that already exists. I hold that under those circumstances we are compelled by an inexorable logic to come to the conclusion that their recommendation as to fresh machinery has been arrived at in an equally hurried manner and is not worthy of being entertained by this House, much respect as I have for every member of the committee who made the representation to us individually. It is not, strictly speaking, a report of the committee at all; the work is done in absolute haste. With regard to any legislation that the Government may bring before us, I shall meet it upon its merits.
I repeat, however, that the Government is in no way debarred from or affected in bringing in that legislation by what this House does in. regard to this report. For these reasons I shall have no hesitation in voting for the amendment of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) that the report be referred back to the committee.
