speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I come from a constituency where there is a very large population and where there is great unrest, and the people have a grievance in connection with the high cost of living, and they look to the Government for some kind of remedy. They look not only for regulation of prices, but for a further investigation into the abuses that are alleged to have occurred throughout the country. Therefore, I agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that it is now up to the Government to introduce legislation first of all providing for the regulation of prices, and second, for a further investigation into the question. It is absolutely necessary in this period of reconstruction that we have lower prices. The first thing that is mentioned in each of these strikes that are taking place in different parts of Canada is the high cost of living, and owing to this wages are being jumped up all the time. Men cannot take care of themselves and their families unless wages are increased or the Government regulates the prices. I am in favour of regulation of prices by the Government, and in the appointment, if necessary, of a court or commission of some kind for that purpose.
I want, however, to point out to the Government that if they appoint a commission, they must go further and make that practically a federal court with all the paraphernalia for the enforcement of federal laws. After fifty years of federal rule in 
this country, the net result of my observations is this: That we have not the necessary machinery to enforce federal law. We ought to have federal courts in this country, and we ought to adopt the same scheme as has been adopted in the United States after all their experiments in federal government. That is, not only must we have federal laws dealing with these questions and a federal court to try them in, but we must impose on the Attorney General or, as we call him in this country, the Minister of Justice, the duty of enforcing these laws. Reference has been	made	to the law
against combines, which law we have had on our Statute Book for a long while, and the Minister of Justice has, on occasions, intervened and attempted prosecutions against combines, hut such action has not been effectively taken, and we ought, therefore, to have on our statute book the same law as they have in the United States, as the result of which they are making substantial progress in the regulation of certain evils that exist in that country. Every law that is passed in the United States contains this clause:
And it shall be the duty of the Attorney General of the United States to enforce this law.
For this purpose a certain sum is provided annually and placed at his disposal for the employment of attorneys, special agents and anything he needs for the purpose of investigating these matters and enforcing the law. Apart from the Exchequer Court, we have no Federal Court in this country. The Exchequer Court could be given jurisdiction to enforce laws of this character, but we must also put in the Criminal Code clauses making it an offence against the Code to profiteer unjustly or to charge exorbitant prices. That may take time, and I grant what has been said in that regard, but it is time we began to do something. The people expect something to be done; something has not been done hitherto, and many things could* be done. The Government cannot escape their responsibility. Even if this legislation does go through, it is possible for the Government to send for representatives of various industries and simply to tell them, as representatives of industries have been told in England:	If you do not reduce your
prices in certain directions, we shall have to interfere. It is true, as has been pointed out, that you might be able to interfere in some respects in connection with the tariff, but I would go further and insert in the Criminal Code clauses defining some

of these offences, such as undue profits and exorbitant prices, which ought to come within the Criminal Code. If we can put two or three of these clauses in the Criminal Code at this session and impose on the Minister of Justice the duty of enforcing the law and have prosecuting attorneys just as there are in the provinces, I believe we shall get substantial results. Some years ago I called the attention of the then Government to the comtoipes that were growing up in this country against the law., I said, " Why do you not enforce the law and prosecute these men?" The answer I got was:	" Go to Mr. Foy," meaning by that
the Attorney General of Ontario. The Attorney General of Canada, that is, the Minister of Justice, is the man who ought to enforce the law.

speechtext:
That is the real issue in this country. If you want to get enforcement of federal law you must do it by your Federal Attorney General, and there must be at least one attorney in each province. Then if these charges are made, if the people feel that they are being unduly taxed and that the high cost of living is something unbearable, as it is to-day to thousands and thousands of people in Canada, you will get some results. It is absurd to follow the practice of the past in regard to combines, namely, to leave the matter to the private prosecutor to enforce a federal law, and no result has so far been attained in this country as against these combines. It is time that these combines were brought under regulation and that the capital of companies was under the jurisdiction of this Parliament. If the plan I have suggested is adopted we can pass an Act at this session which may be effective; it may not cover everything, but it may cover some of these things, and I believe that a substantial reduction of prices will be brought about. There is also the other point, namely, that the Government have the power to summon representatives of various industries to meet them and talk the matter over, and the Government should say to them: You must afford relief of some kind. It is surprising what was done in 'Great Britain in this respect since the beginning of the war by the British Government's sending for representatives of certain industries and telling them: These things are not right; there are over-charges in coal and overcharges in food. The British Government regulated the prices, and that regulation has been effective.
Prices have been reduced because the Government intervened, and they can be reduced in future by defining in the law what is unfair to the public in the matter of prices. I trust that the Government will take effective action in this connection. They are starting in at the tail end of the session, but they have a great amount of information at their disposal not only from this committee but from other sources as well, not to mention the information that Mr. O'Connor -had been able to gather. In view of all these sources of information, we ought to toe able to do something, and the country expects this Parliament to take such action this session as will relieve the distress throughout the country and help to alleviate the unrest attendant on all the strikes. Just consider the condition of the country in connection with these strikes. There was a street railway strike in Winnipeg that lasted four weeks and from which the people suffered a great deal. It was more or less based on the high cost of living. It shifted to Toronto and prevailed there for some ten days, and here in Ottawa now we are experiencing the same kind of strike. Men want more pay all over the country because of the excessive charges which are made for the necessaries of life, and it is the duty of the Government and of Parliament at this time to devise some remedy. It may be late, but "it is never too l-ate to mend," and I think we should do something now. Above all let the Government insert in the Criminal Code a law dealing with this situation. After all, it is the Criminal Code on which I -rely with any confidence, and two or three clauses in that Code defining just what is a profiteer and wh-at are unjust profits would- have an appreciable result. The Criminal Code could define what was illegal in handling the foodstuffs, whether on the part of producers 'or of middlemen, and if the Government have any proposal to make in regard to legislation the people are anxious to be apprised of it and will endorse any measure that will tend to a really satisfactory solution of the problem which faces us to-day.

The committee sat almost day and night, and carried on the inquiry more assiduously, I think, than any committee that was ever appointed by' Parliament, But the hon. gentleman says "The report is wholly immature, it is premature, I do not think the House should act upon it," and then told us in the next sentence that we should have acted on this resolution two years ago.. He said that two years ago an idea of this sort was recommended by Mr. O'Connor and if there is anything in it we should have acted then. Nevertheless, although in his opinion we should have acted two years ago, he claims that the present committee has reached the conclusion too quickly. If the hon. gentleman could not make up his mind in respect to a report brought in on the 26th of June, and he has
had five days since to ponder over the matter and if he is still not able to reach a conclusion after having given five days extra for consideration, what is the use of giving him six, or seven, or eight days? He has already had time to think over the report and suggest any alternative. Has he now any alternative to offer?

subtopic: ADOPTION OF THE ISPEOIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE MOVED.
speechtext:
This question is one of very great importance, and hon. members who are in such haste now to get through with the session would be well advised to take their time. I do not think the country will lose anything if those hon. gentlemen will take their time and deal with this question intelligently. If they so far have done nothing else during the session it is- about time they dealt with this matter, because it undoubtedly is one of the biggest Questions before the country to-day. There is no doubt the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) is absolutely right when he talks about the unrest in Canada. I can point to the cause of the existing unrest, Mr. Speaker, it is attributable to the gentlemen sitting to your right. It is due to the failure on the part of the Government to take action. The feeling of unrest is by reason of the country entertaining the view that the Government has taken absolutely no action with regard to the profiteers. For example, when I asked

a moment ago whether these profiteers, these packing companies, have paid into the treasury the excess in profits which they have taken from the country, the Government is unwilling or unable to answer the question; and hon. gentlemen supporting the Government shout "carried." They are anxious to get home, when it is our business to sit here and legislate for the people. If the country is in such a state of unrest, and every hon. gentleman knows that it is, it is not our business to hurry up and run home, but to sit here and legislate in order to try and satisfy the people and bring about peace and ordeT. It is not our business to fuss around here like a lot of children, but to sdt here and deal with the legislation submitted., whether it is good, bad, or indifferent. There must he a number of causes responsible for bringing about the * present unrest, and if the cost of living in Canada is higher than it should be, legislation should be adopted to bring it down and for that, of course, the Government is responsible. If the boosting of prices to the consumer goes- on in this country, the Gov ernment is responsible for it. I saw a statement in the press, the other day which was credited to the Minister of Finance, although I can hardly believe it. He is reported to have made the statement that inflated currency had nothing to do with the high cost of living. Is that true when we are lending money to foreign countries that are buying our products at thirty per cent less than we pay for those products ourselves? Is that true, when you take into consideration the discount granted to those countries on the bonds of this country and the fact that we are paying thirty-eight per cent more for meat and flour than foreigners are paying for the very same goods exported from this country?
Their bonds are worth seventy-two cents on the dollar and we are taking them at par. The people understand these things, even if the Government do not. There is no doubt that there is great unrest in the country. I want to tell my hon. friends opposite that when a strike breaks out because the people are not getting enough wages to live on and see the big interests pocketing inordinate profits, that it is not the business of the Government to get out their machine guns and see their powder is dry before negotiating; they should negotiate and see what is at the bottom of the trouble. And what that trouble is the Government is being told every day in this House-it is the high cost of living. If this committee has found a solution for the

high cost of living, I think every hon. member will support it, but we have considerable doubts about that. The 'Government appointed a cost of living commissioner last year and the year before, and when the commissioner attempted to bring the profiteers to book, what did the Government do? They had'him dismissed immediately and appointed another commissioner in his place. That other commissioner we have never heard from since. If this commission is- to be a whitewashing commission, if it is simply for the purpose of defending the Government, of course, the people do not want to support it. We do not want to tax the people another $200,000 a year for an unnecessary commission that will do nothing.
My hon. friends on your right, Mr. Speaker, talk of the people paying. They say that the Food Board collected from the people all that it cost the country. Of course, they did. That is exactly what the people are objecting to-paying exorbitant taxes to make jobs for the friends of the Government. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice says that all they collect is a saving to the people, that it goes into the treasury and saves the people in taxes. Why, on that principle the more you tax the people the richer they are. It is the most absurd argument that I have ever heard, and it has been used by hon. members opposite this year and it was also used by them -last year. Other hon. members get up and defend the profiteers. They say that the profits they make would not be very much if distributed among the people. But the profit one man makes, Mr. Speaker, is a guide for others, and before this Cost of Living -Committee we have noticed from day to day that evidence has been brought out of profits from fifty to two hundred per cent being made. Values are relative, and that means that the cost of living is always climbing. The shoe1 merchant who makes sixty per cent is making that profit out of the labouring men ah over the country.
What the people are up in arms about is that the Government is not taking any action to remedy that state of things-and I may tell the Government quite frankly that the people have absolutely no confidence that they will take any action-at least, I have never met any person who has confidence that this Government will curb the profiteers. If the Government are honest and anxious to do what the people want them to do, they have a simple remedy at hand. If they will pass an Order in Council abolishing the War Times Elections Act.
and go to the country on an honest franchise we shall see returned to this House representatives of the people and not representatives of the big interests-a much needed change that will satisfy the people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will only occupy the time of the House two minutes. I want to refer to the objections raised as to the manner in which this resolution was passed. I stated at the outset that a resolution was put before the committee dealing with the principle involved in these recommendations, and that that resolution was carried by the casting vote of the Chairman, But in so far as the regularity of the report is concerned, as it is before the House, a second resolution was put, after the whole committee-those who had voted against the principle and those who had voted for it-had sat down around the tqfcle for an hour and a half and worked out the details of these recommendations. That resolution was moved by Mr. Stevens and seconded by Mr. Douglas, that the recommendations- as finally contained in the second report of the committee be presented to the House on Thursday, the 26th day of June, and was carried on division without any objection whatever.
I wish to refer to another point-the insinuation of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. -Clark) that this report is the result of something done by the Government to induce the committee to take action. I regret that the hon. member should have made that statement, for the reason that it has caused me to lose a very great deal of the regard that I have always had for the hon. member, and the only foundation there can be for any such insinuation is in the diseased imagination of those who are making it. No member of the Government ever approached me, or, as far -as I am able to learn, any other member of the committee in regard to what we should do. When the committee was appointed the Finance Minister, in speaking to me in regard to it, said-: " My desire is that your investigation shall be as wide open as you can make it. Get all the facts you possibly can and present your findings to the House just as you arrive at them." And that is exactly what we did.

I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Marine (Hon. C. C. Ballantyne) to an incident which took place on Sunday last. The Maritime express, with passengers from Canada and United States, including several elderly ladies, left Montreal at the usual hour, 9.25 a.m. When passengers for Murray Bay reached Riviere Ouelle Junction at 5.45 p.m., they found, much to their dismay, that the ferry between Riviere Ouelle and Murray Bay was not running, and several ladies and children were obliged to spend the night at Riviere Ouelle Junction, where there is no hotel; and several of them had to take another train and. return to Quebec. This is a very serious state of affairs, and I aim sure my hon. friend will see to it that whether on Sunday or any other day, when the regular train is advertised to carry passengers as far as Murray Bay, the ferry is available to carry these passengers across the river. House again in Committee on Bill No. 175, relating to the harbour of St. John, in the province of New Brunswick; Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 3-limits of harbour:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are those old limits, or are we taking in new ground ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are taking in a small portion of new ground at Courtenay bay. The city boundary lines do not take in the whole of Courtenay bay, and this Bill is extending the boundary lines so as to take it in.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How much money has the Government spent on Courtenay bay in development up to now?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I could not say offhand- somewhere around $4,000,000, but that is only an estimate. The city of St. John is not selling that portion of Courtenay bay which is not under the Government. The Government is taking that in the harbour limits, and it will be administered by the Board of Harbour Commissioners in order that all wharves and shipping facilities in the city may be under one board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who owns the land around what is known as Courtenay bay? Is it Crown property?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: A portion of it is in the territory of St. John and the other portion is in the parish of "Simonds. The land is all owned by private individuals except the foreshore which is within the limits of the harbour, under the control of the Federal Parliament. Any land which the company took, for instance, for the location of the dry dock which is now under construction, haS been purchased from the various property owners; and any land they may require in the future will also be purchased. The part occupied by the harbour is really altogether within the city limits. The line runs approximately through the centre of what is called the Bay. The wharves, docks, and things of that kind are on the western side, and the dry dock is on the eastern side or in the parish of Simonds.
When will the work be completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I have very good reason to believe the dry dock will be completed in a year and a half and be ready for operation.
Will the dry dock be under control of the Harbour Commission?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
No, it is private property. The company that owns the dock bought the fee of the land from the riparian owners-and are putting up the construction purely as private property.
On section 5-appointments:
Has the Government so' far considered any of the appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Government have not considered who the three commissioners will be, but it is the intention to select well known prominent business men. I hope very shortly to see such men appointed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who are in charge of the harbour? Is it not now conducted under some special supervision?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is being controlled by the city of St. John and will ibe until a formal deed is passed transferring the property to His Majesty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The city of St. John must have a commission. The city as a whole cannot look after the business. Is there a Board of Management now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The city of St. John have what is known as the Commissioner of Docks, Harbours and Ferries and also a harbour master looking after the port of St. John at the present time. Before the city of St. John will be able to say whether they accept or reject the Government offer a referendum will have to be taken, but from what I can learn I do not think there is any doubt about the city being willing to accept the offer the Government is now making of $2,000,000.

made for the payment of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Later on in the
Bill.

4338

speechtext: I am sorry that I am not able to give a definite answer. We will have to consider that.

All subject to a referendum?

speechtext: Right away, t

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

Section 15 says:
The corporation may levy such rates as are fixed by by-law.
We all know what that means, but it is a matter of drafting-rates on what?

Rates on shipping?

speechtext: They formerly were collected by the collector of customs at the port of Montreal,, the shipping people having to deliver their ship's manifest to the customs. I see that the debentures must be in denominations of at least $100. Is that wise? We have, within the last few years, changed the Companies' Act in

order to allow companies to issue debentures for less than $100. It is possible that Government bonds may become more popular as a means of investing the savings of the people of moderate means, and it may be wise to have a denomination of less than $100.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

(4) is the subject of a country which, at the passing of this Act, was at war with His Majesty, provided that such subject was permanently resident in Canada on the fourth day of August in the year one thousand nine hundred and nine.
Is it the pleasure of the Committee to adopt the amendment?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION, AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
I had hoped that the Solicitor General would have had something to say with regard to the amendment before I spoke. When he stated the other evening, after I had submitted the amendment, that it did not appear unreasonable, I had hoped it would be allowed to carry. I do not know what the intention of the Government is with regard to it, although I admit that as an ordinary thing an amendment proposed by a member of the Opposition is not usually received with a great deal of favour. I would say, however, that if it is intended to vote down the amendment, the members of the Committee should realize the gravity of the injustice that in my opinion will be done to certain people living in Canada. The clause in question in its present form will have this effect: That certain men of enemy alien birth, who have lived in this country for a great many years-notwithstanding the fact that they have thought themselves in many instances to be British subjects, and have conducted themselves as such, and notwithstanding the fact, as I said the other day, that some of them had relatives fighting in the Canadian army -would be debarred from becoming naturalized as British subjects for an additional period of ten years. Now, Mr. Chairman, we have not at present in this country too

many good citizens. Furthermore, some weeks ago we passed a new immigration law, which, in my opinion, was just a little too stringent in some respects; and I believe that if this Bill is passed in its present form it will make for a certain amount of unrest among some of the people of Canada consequent upon a feeling of injustice as a result of rendering it impossible for those men to secure that naturalization to which I think they are entitled. Moreover, I believe that if this sort of thing continues- unless the Government has some remedy to offer-a great many responsible and reliable persons, men who are practically citizens of this country and want to do their duty as citizens, will leave Canada, and we can ill afford their loss. A great deal has already been said here with respect to the alien enemy, and I am not going to discuss now the man who technically comes within that class. But it is desirable that men who are at present aliens should become Canadian citizens and good British subjects. We have a great deal of work to do in Canada, we need to develop our resources, and I see no means of meeting the heavy obligation which we have to carry as a result of the war unless that proposition is recognized. Now, although I have no desire to delay the work of the House at this period of the session, I would again lay the salient facts of the situation before the Committee, and more particularly as they affect the constituency of North Waterloo, which I have the honour to represent. It is well known that in the county of Waterloo there are a great many people of either German extraction or German birth, many of whom have lived there for thirty, forty, fifty or sixty years; and I know of one case, coming very closely home to myself, where that residence has extended to seventy-five years.
Most of these people became naturalized in the ordinary course, but hundreds of them are not naturalized to-day for various reasons. First of all, in the years before the war naturalization was not considered of quite so much importance as it is today, and, as was stated in the Order in Council, questions of naturalization were not scrutinized so carefully as they have been since the war began. A good many of these people came to this country as children, they have since grown up to manhood, and many of them were under the impression that their fathers became naturalized under the law shortly after they came to Canada. Their fathers are dead, and many of these men, who are now 	,
thirty or forty or fifty years old, have no means of proving that their fathers were naturalized. Some of those fathers came to Canada even before Confederation, but their sons can show no proof of naturalization. Those men have held public office; they have considered themselves Canadian citizens; all their interests have been incorporated in those of Canada; they have no connection with an enemy alien country now, they really, never had, and many came from Germany before there was any great degree of militarism in that country. On the other hand, a good many of them came to Canada not only because of the opportunities which they thought they would find in this new country, but because they desired to escape from that very militarism.
I think I should refer to one other thing which makes it, perhaps to some extent, Excusable that these men did not take out naturalization papers. I know that possibly some hon. members on the opposite side of the House will say:	If those men
did not think enough of Canada to take out naturalization papers, they should not complain now.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION, AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION, AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
Hon. members say hear, hear; but I would point out to them that among both political parties in the county of Waterloo-as I am sure was also the case in many other sections of Canada where men of German or Austrian nationality had settled-there was a sort of compact that no man when he came to give his vote should be challenged on the score of nationality. You will say that that was wrong; and so it was; but I must again remind the committee that at that time not so much importance was attached to naturalization as has been the case since the war. The result was that these men, not well informed on matters of naturalization-which we now understand a great deal better-were quite content to go on as they were. Their names were always placed on the voters' lists, and they assumed because of that that they were British subjects, and they always voted. That is perhaps merely an excuse, but the fact remains, that those men, having lived in Canada a long time-considering themselves in every way British subjects, and acting in accordance with that belief, are now debarred under this clause from actually receiving naturalization papers.
The Government prior to the last election-I may call it the Borden Govern-

ment-realized that there was some justice in the claim of these,.men to become naturalized, and, as I- said the other day, after a statement had been .made in the House by the right bon. the Prime Minister, the then Government passed an Order in Council under which these men could become naturalized if they could show before a judge that they were worthy of British citizenship. That was in 1917, actually during the war. As a result, some ninety or more [DOT] men in my constituency made application in due form before a judge, the judge passed upon their applications, approved of them, and they were forwarded to the Secretary of State, but absolutely no action of any kind was taken upon them. I might add that it caused me a great deal of surprise yesterday to hear the hon. Secretary of State say that that Order in Council was repealed not so very long ago. I say that because I was in communication with him from time to time with regard to these very men. He assured me again and again that he would bring the matter before the Government, and I believe that that was done, and from time to .time the Government declined to take any action to complete the naturalization, for the reason that the feeling was very strong against anything of that kind being done and they did not think the time was opportune to take action. But I had no intimation whatever that the Order in Council had been repealed, and I had no reason to believe that it would be repealed, and it seems to me that under the circumstances some information might have been given to me in regard to it.
The Solicitor General stated the other evening that he thought the amendment I proposed was not unreasonable, and I am given to understand that the Government is inclined to be sympathetic towards these men, and feels that something should be done. If that is the case I fail to comprehend why this Order in Council was repealed, under which justice could have been done to these men without any interference whatever with the Act which it is now proposed to put on the statute book. If this Bill is passed, as I suppose it will be, T think that the Government in all justice to these men should at least consider naturalizing them, for they in good faith applied for naturalization following action by this Government itself in their behalf. They went to considerable trouble and expense to establish that they were in good faith British subjects in thought and in deed, and they feel, and I think they feel rightly, that the whole thing should be consummated by their being granted naturalization certificates. As it is they are men without a country. They are not German citizens; they have no connection with that land now, and they do not wish to have. They are located in Canada, all their interests are here, and it seems to me that the Government should make naturalization easy for them rather than difficult. I was quite interested yesterday to hear the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) make the statement that naturalization should be given within a year-in fac, that he would force naturalization; I think that was the statement he made. I do not know that I would be prepared to go so far as that, but I do believe that it would be in the interests of the country to give naturalization to men who, upon investigation, have been shown to be worthy of naturalization, instead of making them serve a still longer time. I think we may very well draw a lesson from the action and attitude of the United States in that regard. There men, instead of being disfranchised and prevented from exercising the duties of citizenship, were given every opportunity to become naturalized, and then, and quite fairly, the Government could expect them to carry out the duties incident to citizenship. That seems to me to be much the wiser course.
The only reason that has been advanced, so far as I know, why the amendment which I have submitted should not be adopted is that it would bring our Naturalization Act into conflict with the British Naturalization law, and that the British Government would not accept as evidence of Imperial citizenship any certificate issued under >an Act amended by the clause which I have proposed.
With all due regard, to that statement, I find it difficult to believe that the British Government would decline to recognize a naturalization certificate issued by this Government if this Government had satisfied itself, as would be its duty, that the persons so naturalized were fit subjects for naturalization. Surely the British Government must realize that conditions in Canada are different from what they are in England. After all, why should not Canada legislate for herself? Nobody proposes that the Canadian Parliament, which is an autonomous Parliament-and we are told that we are a nation-should interfere with British legislation, with British naturalization, so far as Britain herself is concerned; and it seems to me that in this matter Canada should be, autonomous; Canada should not do an injustice to any class of
4.342

the people for the sake of agreeing in every respect with the demands of British law. I repeat that we should legislate for ourselves and see that no injustice is done to people who in fact belong to our own country.
I am supported in this belief by the action of the Imperial War Conference, which was mentioned here yesterday. I do not know how often that conference met or what were its final decisions, but I hold in my hand what professes to be a verbatim report of a meeting held in the summer of 1918, as published in the Evening Telegram of Toronto, on March 31, 1919. At that conference, which was attended by representatives from Canada, in the person of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell); from Newfoundland, from India, South Africa, New Zealand and Australia, the following resolution was adopted:
This conference is iof the opinion that legislation should be passed throughout the Empire restricting for a period after the war, sp far as in the circumstances of each country may be possible, the naturalization of citizens of present enemy countries and also the acquisition by them of any form of political rights or of land or of mining privileges.
That resolution was carried, but only after a very considerable discussion. I am going to quote some of the things that were said; they bear directly upon this discussion. Sir George Cave, who, I think, was the representative of the British Colonial Office-

speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to reply just on that one point? When that discussion came up at the Imperial Conference, we understood that the Home Secretary intended inserting that clause to which he referred, limiting the rights of naturalization, in the section relating solely to Great Britain, but apparently, as I understand from the Solicitor General, he inserted it in the part which relates to the whole Empire, and that creates the difficulty at the present time. Undoubtedly the attitude of the Canadian representatives was, as my hon. friend has intimated in the extracts he has read.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION, AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: Would I be right in stating that the Bill as it stands now is not really in harmony with the feelings of the Prime Minister and the President-of the Council with regard to these matters? May I ask if, feeling as they do-and I must assume that what I have read here is correct with regard to their attitude-there is any intention on the part of the Government to take any action that will relieve the situation as I have outlined it with regard to these men?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION, AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
I entirely adhere to the view which. I expressed at the conference, but the question at the present time is in respect of legislation which is designed to have its effect, through common action of the Empire's parliaments, not only throughout Canada, but throughout the whole Empire. If we should accede to the hon. gentleman's amendment, I do not know what the effect would be on all certificates of naturalization which might be hereafter granted in this country. It would establish a distinct divergence from the Imperial Act. Hon. gentlemen who have studied this question at all know that the purpose of the resolution at the Imperial Conference of 1911 was to secure such uniformity of legislation that certificates of naturalization granted in one part of the Empire would be effective throughout the whole Empire. For that reason the measure which was the outcome of the conference resolution was submitted to every Dominion of the Empire. It was adopted by Canada. We had a great deal of negotiation and discussion both oral and by cable with regard to some of its provisions before we reached a common conclusion. Eventu-

ally, the Act was passed in 1914 by the United Kingdom and in the same year by Canada, and along precisely the same lines. In 1918, the British Government, doubtless under the stress of a very powerful and even vehement public opinion, introduced certain amendments.
As the President of the Privy Council pointed out, we did not understand during the Imperial Conference last summer that the particular proposal upon which I spoke was to be included in that part of the British Act which related to the whole Empire and1 which should be the foundation of common legislation throughout the Empire; and so I expressed myself as I did. I think it will be necessary to pass the Act in its present form, but I assure my hon. friend that I will make representations to the British Government with respect to the matter with a view to having such modifications made in the Imperial Act as will permit of reasonable modification in our own.
Amendment negatived.	.
