speechtext: Will the minister explain the object of this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The object of the Bill,
as I explained on the first reading, is to enable the Civil Service Commission to appoint to permanent positions in the Civil Service persons who were taken on temporarily at Winnipeg, Calgary, and Saskatoon, and in the railway mail service, to replace employees who retired from the postal service in the month of May last. The members of the House will recall that on the 15th May the employees of the Winnipeg post office, with few exceptions, went out on a sympathetic strike that was then called in the city of Winnipeg. On, I think, the morning of the 24th of May, a notice was published in the public press of Winnipeg, notifying the employees then on strike that unless they returned to their work before noon on Monday 26th May, their places would be permanently filled. I am instructed that personal notices were also sent out by the postmaster at Winnipeg to all the employees to the same effect. I might say that before this date, in order that the. public service might be maintained and the carriage of His Majesty's mails continued, the postmaster at Winnipeg had been authorized by the Postmaster General to secure the necessary employees to carry on the work. He pointed out that it was difficult, if not impossible, to obtain these temporary employees, unless he was

in a position to guarantee them permanent employment. They were largely returned soldiers, and they were only willing to take the positions, under the conditions which then prevailed, if they could be assured that their appointment would, be permanent. The postmaster at Winnipeg communicated this information to the Postmaster General, and for the reasons already stated the Postmaster General assured the postmaster of Winnipeg that he might promise permanent employment to the persons in question, subject, of course, to Parliament's sanctioning such action. This Bill therefore is to enable the Civil Service Commission to appoint to permanent positions the men who were taken on under those conditions in the city of Winnipeg.
Then, in the city of Calgary, about the same date-that is, some time between the 15th and 24th of the month-information came to the Postmaster General that there was danger of the employees in the Calgary post office going out on a sympathetic strike with the postal employees at Winnipeg. Accordingly he sent the following telegram:
Regret to learn everything points to sympathetic strike with Winnipeg on part of postal workers. Government considers such action wholly unwarranted and in violation of the plain duty of postal employees. The Prompt handling of His Majesty's mails and the maintenance of the public postal service at this time is the first obligation of every employee under the Post Office Department. For such employees to seek to embarrass or prevent the prompt handling of His Majesty's mails by a sympathetic strike is entirely incompatible with loyal service to the country and all postal "employees joining in a sympathetic strike will be deemed to have resigned their positions in His Majesty's service and their places will be promptly filled. All loyal employees will be supported and protected by the Government. Make known to employees and keep department promptly informed.
I am advised by the Postmaster General that that telegram was communicated to the employees of the Calgary post office, and they were urged to remain at their post and not to go out on strike in sympathy with the general strike in Winnipeg. Notwithstanding that, however, they chose to go out, and the Post Office Department, acting upon that telegram, took the ground that they had resigned their positions in the public service, and the postmaster at Calgary was authorized to fill their places. He did so, and I understand seventy per cent or more of the new employees are returned soldiers.
I need not go into the somewhat similar conditions which prevailed at Saskatoon. At that city the postal employees went out without having received the same specific 
warning as the employees at Calgary, and they were given a certain time within which to return. I understand that in Saskatoon a very large number did return. Further, the railway mail clerks in Winnipeg went out on a sympathetic strike, but all returned within the time limit. Certain of the railway mail clerks at Saskatoon also went out on a sympathetic strike. Several returned wit'hin the time specified, but a few did not.
The Bill now before the House covers appointments in Winnipeg, , Calgary, and Saskatoon and in the Railway Mail Service, and it authorizes the Civil Service Commission, on the recommendation of the Deputy Postmaster General, to appoint to the permanent staff:
(a)	any employee who was temporarily taken on to the staff and employed In the Post Office or in the Railway Mail Service at any one of the cities of Winnipeg, Saskatoon or Calgary to replace employees who ceased to perform their duties in the said offices or in the said service in May, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen, and
(b)	any temporary employee in any one of the said Post Offices or in the Railway Mail Service at the said cities who did not absent themselves from duty in the, said Post Offices or in the said Service, in the month of May, or who were absent from their duties in the said month but returned thereto within the time limited for so doing.
Then the Bill provides:
No age limit shall apply in the case of any such appointment, and it shall not be necessary for any person so appointed to pass or to have passed any Civil Service Examination, provided such person is certified by the Postmaster of the city where the person is to be employed or by the Superintendent of the Railway Mail Service, as the case may be, to be competent and fit to do work for which he is required.
I sav without hesitation, Mr. Chairman, that we should not depart from the principles of the Civil Service Act and authorize appointments by statute, as we are now doing, except under circumstances of the most urgent character. And it was only the urgency of the situation, and the importance of keeping the mail service in operation, that justified the Postmaster General authorizing the postmasters, of these cities to take on^these employees, with the assurance .that their appointments would be made permanent on the conditions mentioned in the Bill.

I understand that when the postmasters of Winnipeg, Calgary and Saskatoon found that they had no one to sort and deliver letters, and so on, they opened their respective offices to these volunteers. By this legislation you are going

to make those men permanent employees. I have no objection to that. I think it is wise that men who offered their services when the Government was in need of them, and when it was dangerous for them to render assistance, should certainly be appointed permanently. But how will they be classified? For instance, a man may have been appointed temporarily as a sorter or a letter carrier who would be fit for a higher position in the service, and, consequently, would command a higher salary. It would not be fair for such a man in this rush to be assigned to a position inferior to that which his abilities would enable him to fill. Therefore I would like to be enlightened on that point by my hon. friend.
The next point I wish to call to his attention is this. The members of the Committee no doubt have received to-day a circular letter signed, I think, by Mr. Tulley, of Ottawa, secretary of the Civil Service Federation. In that letter he makes an appeal to the Prime Minister on behalf of the men who went on strike. I, for one, do not wish to give an opinion on this matter, but I would like to know if the reasons on which this appeal is based are found sufficiently weighty by the right hon. gentleman to favourably consider the case of those men. It is stated-and it would have appealed to me very forcibly if I had been Postmaster General-that many a poor wife will suffer from the fact that the father and husband was, so to speak, forced to strike. I wish to remind the House that I do not adopt this plea as my own; I am simply repeating offhand what is stated in the letter. It is represented that many of those men, indeed the majority of them, would not have left their duties if they had not been under threat of reprisals on the part of a large, body of strikers. Now the strike is at an end, "Order reigns in Varsovie," as was said of old-peace is established in Winnipeg, and an appeal is made to the right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) to consider favourably the case of these unfortunate letter-carriers and sorters. I would like to know if he intends to take any action on that appeal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have a very deep sympathy indeed for the position in which these men find themselves.
My right hon. friend received that letter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have received the letter, and I have seen the representatives of the postal employees of the West.
I have given the best consideration I could to their case and have given them an answer. If one yielded to his sympathy, naturally, he would be inclined to say that these men, although misled, might be given another opportunity. But I ask the Committee to recall the circumstances which confronted this country when these men went out on sympathetic strike.
I have already stated the facts in this House, and I need not repeat them. The situation was, perhaps, somewhat more serious than most hon. gentlemen in this House are inclined to believe or able to realize. I am thoroughly confident that if the Government had not taken the position which it did at the outset, the postal service would have been absolutely demoralized not only in the cities which have been mentioned, but also in other western cities, and perhaps in eastern cities as well. The condition in which these men find themselves is absolutely of their own choice. They went out on strike in Winnipeg without any notice to the Government. I am not concerned at the moment with the precise reasons which induced them to take that course, but I have understood from their representatives that it was through their having joined, without the consent of the Government, some organization in February last, the behest of which they felt themselves bound to obey rather than the lawful commands of the Government of this country. The Government of Canada and ' the people of Canada are not responsible for the course which they took in joining ax; organization of that kind. Nevertheless, even when they did go out on sympathetic strike in Winnipeg, they were not dismissed; they were given nearly three days within which to return to their duty and were distinctly notified that if they did return to their duty they would be reinstated in the place in the service which they had previously held.- About seventy of them,
I think, did Teturn; the others felt themselves constrained to obey the commands of the organization which they had joined in this way. That was an absolutely deliberate choice on their own part.
So far as Calgary and Saskatoon are concerned, the conditions were very much the same. At Calgary, distinct notice was given to the postal employees that if they saw fit to abandon their public duty and obey the command of the organization which they had joined-in all these cases for the purposes of a sympathetic strike and not in respect of any grievances of their own-then they might regard themselves as permanently retired from the postal ser-

vice. I venture to think, after the most careful consultation with pry colleagues and after the best consideration which I have been able to give the case Of these men, that it is absolutely impossible for the Government to recede from that attitude, which I have announced over and over again in this House. I am sorry that I am forced to that conclusion, but the public interest does force me to it and to no other.
I might say that conditions within the past year were becoming somewhat acute from time to time in the Civil Service in Ottawa itself. Although I was absent from the country for ten months immediately preceding my return on the 25th of May last, I did hear murm-urihgs and suggestions that there were going to be strikes here in the Civil Service at Ottawa. I think it is high time that men invested with public duties as civil servants of Canada at Ottawa or elsewhere should learn that that is not the way in which their grievances are to be remedied.

If at a given moment during that very serious strike it became dangerous for public officials to remain at their posts-if, say, they were threatened- that might be a consideration which would weigh in their favour. I do not say that that was the case, but it is alleged in the appeal which has been made to the right hon. gentleman that those unfortunate postal employees were forced to join the strike. I myself do not know the facts of the case, but I should like to know from the Prime Minister whether that allegation has been investigated so that the reply of the Government to this appeal may not lose some of its weight through the fact that these employees acted under duress.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Seventy men in Winnipeg did return to their duty, and were protected in the performance of that duty. Besides that, a number of men, referred to in this Bill, entered the public service and have performed the duties which were abandoned by the employees who went on strike; they also were protected in the performance of their duty. I cannot, therefore, bring myself to believe that any idea of duress or of danger actuated any of these employees.

The statement we have heard from my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) has been ' useful in that it has cleared up one or two possible misapprehensions. I recognize, as I am sure every

member of this House does, that the Government had a condition of very great difficulty to deal with and that it was their clear duty to carry on the public service of the country. We are all agreed up to that point. No one, at any rate, can charge the Government with want of courage in the attitude they are taking; they are clearly seeking not for popularity, hut for the public good as they see it. I gladly concede that and claim it for the Government. I was interested to hear the Prime Minister say 'that the fact that the union which the men had joined involved the acceptance by the men of the principle of the sympathetic strike was without the knowledge of the Government, because it was tolerably clear in my mind that if the men had joined a union- which contained a clause permitting them to ad-opt the sympathetic strike, that would have been- the time for the -Government to interfere. But when we hear from my right- hon. friend that the Government did not know that that plank was in the platform of the postmen's union-, then very clearly the Government are absolved from all blame, except, perhaps, that some captious critics would say they ought to have known.
With regard to the present attitude of the men, the Prime Minister does not need to assure the House that he is personally sympathetic with the individual men affected; I am sure that every one in this country will accept that statement. Every one will also be alive to the fact that it would be impossible to make room for the men and take them back, without displacing men who have stepped in to serve the country in what my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has called its time of difficulty.
But there is a broader, view of this question which appeals to my mind-. The Winnipeg strike is over; I hope all that trouble is over. But he is a sanguine citizen of Canada who does not anticipate very considerable labour troubles in the next two years. I very much fear that post-war conditions will be aggravated at some period in that time and probably in an increasing degree during that time. I see no reason, in the present condition of parties- in this country, why this Government should not be in power for that time, and I should say that a wise government, looking ahead, would base their action towards those men not entirely nor chiefly on the ground oi what is coming to the men, but on the ground of what their action would likely be in enabling them to deal with the difficult times through which the country is

passing. From my study of human nature, I think the Government would be in a stronger position if they did not take a stonewall attitude towards those men. If there were vacancies they could be filled by those men. If the service could be helped by the return of a certain number of men, then I do not think it would be a sign of weakness, -but a sign of foresightedness and moral courage to recede from a position which was taken'in the midst of a strike, to the extent of filling any of those vacancies in a fair way from the men who acted upon this plank in their platform, as they themselves tell us, in the belief that that plank was known to be in their platform by the Government whom they ,were serving. I do not need to say any more upon the subject to make my position perfectly clear. Firmness and courage are great qualities in this world, but in the government of peoples in difficult times, I am perfectly certain, the qualities of firmness and courage will carry us further if they are associated with qualities of a different character. It has been said that the greatness of human character is in a due admixture of firmness and gentleness. Every one of us who has had to do with young people or in the government of others, even in a small degree, knows how much it is necessary to mix these qualities in handling our fellow men over whom we have a species of surveillance and employership.
(Mr. MEIGHEN: I cannot permit the recommendation of the hon. member from Red Deer (Mr. iM. Clark) to pass without a word as to the application of the principles of firmness and courage, tempered, as he says, with the opposite qualities, in respect of the present circumstances. In the first place, it is difficult for my simple mind to understand how firmness and courage can very well be tempered with weakness and vacillation; but I am quite aware that firmness and fairness walk well together, and must ever be associated if Government or any other system of human affairs is to be properly conducted. But I am not able to understand how any principle of fairness is to be served by the adoption of the course that my hon. friend recommends in this instance. He tells us that the postal employees in Winnipeg belonged to some organization, and that they claimed that the principles of that organization compelled them to abandon the service of the State in response to the command of outside constituted officers aliei to the Government and to organized public 276
thought, and that their being bound in that organization, was something known to the Government. 1 think that the hon. member for Red Deer might take it for granted that no Government, fit to remain outside of solitary confinement, would be likely to acquiesce in the terms of a union which bound servants of the State to break, at the command of heads of that union, their oath of office and their clear and manifest duty of service to the State that paid them.
(Mr. M. CLARK: I hope my hon. friend appreciates the fact that I accepted, without any reservation, the statement of 'the Prime Minister that that was so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will then proceed on the assumption that any obligations repugnant to their oath of office and clear duty these men entered into, were wholly unknown to the Government. In the light of that established and admitted truth, what is the duty in the circumstances? In Winnipeg, >by reason of the action of the postal employees, we found a city of 250,000 people denied the services to which they were entitled, for which they had paid, without which they were not able to carry on their ordinary avocations, and in the absence of which, indeed, all commercial business was paralyzed, and the whole city was placed at the mercy of a dictatorship with which these postal employees were allied. What was to be done? Relying on the allegiance of these men, on their fidelity to their oath and their manifest duty, an organization had been built up, and the heads of that organization advised us that, without at least a fair proportion'of the trained men, it would be a long and difficult task for them to build up a new personnel that would enable them to carry on the business; that anything approaching a totally new personnel in a post office organization would require days, weeks and even months before they could render any service to the State. Obviously, the only way in which the services of the State could be rehabilitated was by taking some step which would have the effect throughout the Dominion not only of asserting once and for all the authority of constituted Government, but of bringing back for the time being such a proportion of those trained men as would enable them, associated with new employees, to carry on. Some such step as that was the only one that would meet the menacing circumstances that confronted us. What was to be done? The only course possible that would bring results was to say to all and sundry who were concerned



that, unless they returned to the posts which they should never have deserted- which they deserted without any cause appertaining to themselves whatever, which they deserted after notice and after admission by themselves that they i had no grievance-those posts would be occupied by others who would be engaged on a permanent basis, and they would be once and for all dismissed from the public service. Nothing but a strong step could possibly have had any chance of success. Anything in the nature of a weak step or of compromise had no chance of success whatever. Is there any hon. gentleman who will controvert that statement? Therefore, this step was taken. A notice was sent to the house of every person who was employed in the postal service, that unless he came back before twelve o'clock on the 26th, he could not hope thereafter to be employed.
Every means was taken to insure that that notice reached them twenty-four hours or thereabouts before the time for return was fixed, and they were told, once for all, that unless they did return by that date and resume their duties, they could not hope thereafter to be employed. The Provincial Government took exactly the same step and made the same pronouncement in regard to their telephone service. What happened in the meantime?-and this is an important circumstance to be remembered. During the forenoon of the twenty-sixth of December the heads of this movement, which in Winnipeg aspired to the erection of a Soviet Government in that city as a demonstration to the rest of Canada, established themselves on the streets of Winnipeg in the rear of the posit office and at the corners of the streets in the neighbourhood and proclaimed to the men who sought to return and do their duty, as they know they should, that the Government of this country was not sincere and would not carry out its pledged word. They said: The Government is trying to get you back, but it does not mean what it says when it tells you that you will not be re-employed. Mr. Evens, of unhappy memory, Mr. Winning, Mr. Pickup, and others of that ilk, stationed themselves at strategic points in the neighbourhood and preached the certainty of vacillation on the part of the Government of Canada, in the hope thereby to encourage men to defy the law and authority [DOT]and refrain from returning to duty. Now, what is the request made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), and the,hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux)?

It simply is to vindicate the prophecies of Ivens, Winning and Pickup, and make it clear that this Government was indeed only bluffing and did not mean what it said. Fairness, firmness and strength, tempered with opposite qualities, said the hon. member. Yes, if that course is to be pursued and the preaching of Mr. Pickup and Mr. Ivens is to be vindicated by the action of Parliament, and if their prediction that the Government, merely bluffing, would not act, is to be fulfilled, what is going to result? No matter what troubles we may have in this Dominion, no matter who may desert his post, though hundreds, yea thousands, may leave the service of the State and paralyze the whole public business of the country, the preachers of that doctrine will be- able to say, with all authority, to those who fail to realize their responsibility: "The Government is only bluffing. They bluffed in May, 1919, and they are bluffing still and will not keep their word." If that- should come to pass the word of the Government would be entirely disregarded. It is not that there is no sympathy with the men who were made the dupes of those orators. There is sympathy for them. As I witnessed man after man pressing forward to listen to the harangues of the Red leaders that morning, I knew that the time would come when men with wives and families would be appealing to the authorities and to the Government, on grounds of sympathy, to be reinstated. But I knew at the same time that reinstatement would mean the prostitution of the word of this Government and would discount and destroy the word of any Government in days to come, and that though it would be difficult to deny those men something in the way of charitable consideration, there was a greater purpose to be served, namely, the preserving of the foundation of law and order in Canada and the vindication of the fact that when Government makes a pronouncement it means it and intends to stick to it, come what may. The question now is as to whether we will uphold our word or recede, whether there is anything in the nature of firmness and consistency in the attitude of the Government, oi whether it is to be lightly receded from and, in effect, reversed, on the plea of generosity-but really out of timidity and vaccil-lation.	,

At the time the Winnipeg postal men and the postal men ' in Calgary went out on strike, were they aware of the usurpation of civil authority

by the soviet element on the strike committee?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was manifest on the streets and in the shop windows of the city from end to end. The assertion of soviet authority was evident everywhere, and those men must have known it, if there was any possible way of bringing it to their minds.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We are dealing with a very important question. Far be it from me, as a member of this House, to take any. attitude that would be subversive of the principles of sound administration and proper governmental discipline in this or, indeed, in any other country. But governments, like individuals, should seek to set good examples, and if the government of a country in dealing with its subjects fails to set good examples, it rather tends to weaken the authority not only of the government itself but of all its officials. I was preached at last night from every quarter of the Government side of the House, because I found fault with what I regarded as a recognition of the breaking of a very solemn and holy command which is binding upon us all. I was defending a high moral principle underlying the very foundation of the family life of the country, and was saying that the sanctity of the marriage tie should not be violated. Almost every one on the Government side flew at me and declaimed that it was greater to be merciful, generous and broad; that this attitude was far greater than abiding by the laws of God and the commandments which were handed down to us from Moses and the Prophets. It appears that mercy is to be shown only to such characters as we were dealing with last night-'persons who violate every law and principle of good morals in this country. Such characters are to be taken up tenderly and handled with care by the Government and Parliament, and all their sins are to be washed away. They are to be regarded as faultless and whiter than snow. But when we come to deal with erring man, he is to be wiped off the face of the earth. We have the commandment of God, on the one hand, and the commandment of the Minister of the Interior on the other. We can afford with impunity to disobey the command of God, but we are damned at once if we disobey the commands of the Minister of the Interior. I would like to know how often my good friend the minister heard from the citadels, the ramparts and the walls of Zion, the glad tidings of
276i
salvation offered to him to return as a repentant sinner. Has he come back yet? What would he think if he were condemned because he did not come back after the very first sermon he heard? We must not forget that when we are dealing with men who are wrought up as strikers are, we are dealing with humanity in its very worst frame. Under such circumstances we are dealing with humanity in a temper that renders it least prepared for any compromise or sane conclusions. The great jurist Blackstone told us, as is found in his Commentaries, that when we construe law or deal with men we must understand at once that we are not dealing with machines but with humanity, and that we must construe our laws and shape our conduct in the light of that knowledge. I said at the outset that governments were bound to set good examples. What would the Government say if any company in Winnipeg; after the strike was over, said to all their employees:	We have- given you
offers to come back; we have, been coaxing you to come back for the last month; you refused to come; you refused to receive our offers and proposals to you; you did the best you could; now you cannot hold out any longer, not one of you will put his nose inside of any work of ours; you can go elsewhere, and that is the end of it. The Government would not tolerate that sort of thing. The Government would say to any employer of that kind: You must deal fairly with the men; you will have to take them back; you will have to recognize the conditions of this country; they must be observed and we shall see to it that such laws shall be made as will compel you to treat fairly with these men. That is the position that we would expect any Government to take. But what would that employer say to my Tight hon. friend the Prime Minister to-day if they should expect him to consent to any conditions of that kind? He would say, "Ah, yoii are talking that way now but what did you do? You took a few servants in the post office who refused to dc exactly what you wanted them to do and, because they did not do what you wanted them to do, you wiped them out of existence and would not take one man back; yet you come to us and tell us that we must forget everything while you forget nothing." That is the position in which the Government finds itself to-day. It is a hard thing for a proud Government to come down from its pedestal and admit that it must behave like an ordinary employer, but after all the members of the Government are just ordinary human beings-perhaps a little more

than ordinary, but they are just men. We hope they are men, and if they are they must come down from their pedestal and say to these post office employees:	You
behaved badly, you should not have gone out on strike, you should have stayed at your posts; but now this thing is all over, we hope better judgment will guide you in the future, we will give you one more chance ; go back to your work, and see that you do not commit such grave mistakes again. That is the course which the Government should have taken.
In the great city of Winnipeg we heard of those thousand men on a committee who were relieving the distressed conditions in which the city found itself. Now that the strike is over the gentlemen who were serving on that committee cleaning up the streets and working in the post office have gone back to their own occupations. There is not one of them, in so far as we know, who has said to the authorities in Winnipeg that they must make their positions permanent, or who has asked that they discharge these regular employees and give them their places. It was understood that the men who were on strike were to be taken back. It is all very well to be firm. The Government find it easy to be firm when they are dealing with a few strikers in the post office service. They were not quite so firm when, in the last two years, they were dealing with the profiteers of this country. Thpre was no great firmness displayed on that occasion. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) was quite willing to turn a corner in connection with this situation and get out of the way. He was not very brave in facing these wealthy profiteers who are the masters of the situation and masters of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman referring to this afternoon's vote?
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That remark about this afternoon's vote may bring a laugh, but if any body thinks I gave any wrong vote this afternoon he is highly welcome to think so. I cannot appreciate the laugh. All the hon. the Minister of the Interior has td do is to stand up and smile, and there are a lot of people who will dance to his music. I venture to think that there is not one person here who knows what he meant by " this afternoon's vote." We will pass that over. He blames the post office employees for entering into an association for the purpose of bargaining; but, he has bargained

with splendid effect when certain gentlemen will laugh and dance to his music. I say that the Government found it easy to be firm with these few poor, helpless men who were entirely under their control; they were not so firm in other places where they ought to have been firm. I can say to the Prime Minister that it is not yet too late to recast this hard-and-fast rule which he seems to have laid down for himself. I do not think it is his rule. I think it is the rule of the hon. gentleman with the big stick, who went to Winnipeg, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), determined to have his way, and who was prepared from the beginning to wade right through Winnipeg or anything else that stood in his way in order to maintain his will and crush everything that stood in his path. He prides himself on being the author of very drastic legislation in this country, and he now prides himself on having crushed these few poor fellows under his control in the Post Office Department. He can boast of another achievement in having persuaded the Prime Minister to stand behind him in the position which he has taken. I shall not detain the House one moment longer than to remind the House that yesterday we were talking of the woman who was trying to pass herself off as a man's wife when she was not his wife. Some hon. gentlemen were willing to call her his wife and to give her the privileges of a wife and to cast no stones in that direction; but here we find that they have reserved their fusilade of ammunition for a group of poor civil servants in the post office who happened to take one wrong step.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the privilege of saying a word in regard to this matter for the reason that there is a phase of this whole subject that it would seem to me .the House and the country have not been seized of,' notwithstanding all that has been said and written in regard to the Winnipeg strike. In the first place let me say that there was no such thing as a strike in the accepted sense of the term in Winnipeg. There was an organized, carefully planned and carefully worked out effort on the part of a group of exceedingly clever men to destroy everything in the shape of constituted authority in this country, and to destroy what they professed to uphold-organized labour itself. We have heard a good deal in regard to the fact that the postal authorities joined these organizations the constitution of which contained a clause per-

mitting them to take part in a sympathetic strike. It has not been my privilege to read the constitution of the organization to which the postal employees belonged.
But I want to say this, as one who knows something of organized labour: That a sympathetic strike in itself is a direct contradiction of the principle that the strike in Winnipeg was supposed to be called to uphold, namely, the right of collective bargaining. There can be no such thing as collective bargaining, there can be no organization founded on the principle of collective bargaining, that recognizes a sympathetic strike. Collective bargaining must stand or fall on the inviolability of a contract and there can be no such thing as the inviolability of a contract where a sympathetic strike is recognized. So that any plea that is put forward on behalf of the postal employees that they belonged to a legitimate body of organized labour that had within itself the germ or genesis of a sympathetic strike falls to the ground at once.
But I want to pass on to another phase of the question, and to refer particularly to what the leader of the Opposition has said as to the attitude that a private company would take with regard to its employees, under circumstances similar to that in which the Government finds itself with respect to these postal employees. Now, what has taken place in the city of Winnipeg in connection with regularly constituted bodies of organized labour? The Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Engineers and the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen will be recognized, I think, as fairly well established bodies of organized labour. It became known to these organizations very early in the so-called Winnipeg strike that an effort was being made to bring local pressure to bear on the membership of these two local organizations in Western Canada to draw them into a sympathetic strike, and their leaders immediately went to Western Canada in order to see that the members of the organizations should fulfil their contracts and abide by the constitutions of the organizations to which they belonged. Notwithstanding their efforts, what occurred? I do not know how many postal authorities there were, but 500 men in the train service in Western Canada violated their contracts, refused to be guided by the leaders of the organizations to which they belonged, and went out on strike. What happened? Was there any sympathy shown for these men that has been pleaded for to-night in connection with the postal employees? Did the railway companies that these men were
employed by take them back in a body, or did the organizations to which they belonged recognize the right of these men to violate their contracts at will and violate the obligations that they were under to their organizations? Not for one moment. Every single one of the 500 men were expelled from these organi-ations and their leaders themselves undertook to say " We will replace every man who violates his contract." That is the position, Sir, that those men are in to-day.
Having gone that far, however, I wish to say something as regard to what I believe took place with regard to these 500 men, and in that connection there is a thought that the Government might take into consideration in considering the case of the postal employees. There has been, ever since I have known anything about organized labour on the North American continent, what is known as a black list, a list on which the name of a man goes when he is put in a position where he cannot be recognized as fit to be given employment by one of the recognized railway organizations, and by the large employers of labour under whom that very class worked. But the 500 men to whom I refer will not, in my judgment, be placed on any such black list. It will be recognized that local pressure possibly carried them off their feet. They will be punished for having done what they did, by losing their membership in their organizations and their positions with the companies by whom they were employed, but they will he permitted, one by one, as opportunity may arise, to reenter the service as new men. I want to say that in my judgment the Government has absolutely vindicated the position that it took in connection with the Winnipeg strike and in particular relation to the postal employees; and I say further, as a member of a body of organized labour- and I believe that all right-minded members of organized labour from one end of the country to the other will bear me out in doing so-that organized labour was, and is, behind the Government in the position it took in Winnipeg. But, having vindicated that position absolutely and clearly, the Government will not be necessarily receding from that position if it treats these men not as persons on the black list but as men who may re-enter the service as new men starting one by one from the bottom up should occasion arise, and that is as far as any man can legitimately ask the Government to go. I would say to the Government, it will be well advised to simply treat the group of men who were misled

in the situation in which they find them

selves in Winnipeg, as though they had never been in the postal service at all, as new men coming forward and making application for a position without anything in the nature of a black list being held against them.

I desire to say a few words with regard to this subject which affects the city of Calgary, a portion of which I represent. At the time the postal clerks saw fit to leave their work in that city, out of 208 employees in the office, 207 did not report for duty on the next day or following days, and the result of their walk-out was a very serious matter to the city of Calgary, to Western Canada, and to the Dominion as a whole. I believe they were badly led, and were ill-advised, in their action. At the time the strike vote was taken, 128 men voted to go out and 42 voted to remain at >
their posts, and some others were away on'their vacation. Upon the occasion of my visiting the city of Calgary in connection with this matter, and since my return here, I was requested by various organizations to intercede for the reinstatement of: those men in their former positions. And here let me, say, with respect to the remarks of the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) I regret that when he is discussing what is a fair and square issue he does not come out on a very definite line and say exactly what his position is. The reinstatement of those men resolved itself into two questions: First, shall they be reinstated in accordance with the request of their officials-that is, shall every man be returned to his pqsitxon and receive his former rank and seniority? When I was in the city of Calgary and when I accompanied the delegation that waited upon the Government, I made my position very clear on that point-I will not advocate the reinstatement of those men in their former position because of the fact that many persons have been enlisted into the service of the post office in the city of Calgary to take 'the places of the strikers, and it would necessitate the discharge or displacement of those men and throwing them out on the street if those who had wilfully violated their duty to their country were reinstated. The men who have been appointed to fill the positions of the strikers are entitled to as much and even more consideration at the hands of the Government, than those men who were misled and deceived, and who deliberately walked out and closed up the post office in Calgary. But, while they cannot be reinstated in their former posi-LMr. Nicholson.^
tions, I have taken the stand with the Prime Minister, the Acting Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Labour, that there are many good and faithful servants in the Calgary post office who were misled.
They have been taught a lesson, and they could be returned to their positions in the post office, where they would render splendid and faithful service to the country, and it would be a betterment for the service. I think it is only fair to some of those men that they should be allowed to make their application for re-engagement and take the consequence of the lesson which they have learned. I cannot agree with the Acting Minister of Justice that this would be regarded as a policy of vacillation. Those men would make their applications as new men;.they would not be reinstated at the dictates of any organization which caused them to violate their oath of office with the Government; they would be given exactly the same positions and the same standing that would be given to any other applicants. I trust that in .*the near future the Government will again take this matter under consideration and give to many of those men an opportunity to apply for employment in the Civil Service.

I would ask to speak for a double purpose, Mr. Chairman: First, to refute some things that have been said by the leader of the Opposition, and, second, to deal with my friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson). When my friend from Algoma says that collective bargaining knows no such things as a sympathetic strike, it is apparent that he has not followed the labour question to any great extent. Collective bargaining has been recognized as long as individual bargaining: and the sympathetic strike has also been recognized as long as striking has been recognized, as a weapon for labour to secure something that it could not otherwise secure. The only distinction I wish to make in this respfect is that the sympathetic strike has been condemned where the motive underlying it has been absolutely wrong. Kecently I read a book published in England in which it was stated that during this war peeresses and factory girls worked together in the munition factories, and ordinary labourers and peers fought together in the trenches; but now that the war is over we are asking the common people to go back to the degrading employments which they were engaged in before the war after having worked and fought to save their country and the Empire. The

writer advises: You must deal with labour more generously than you have in the past. I wonder whether this Government has not been remiss in its duty to the extent of not advising the capitalistic class that they must be more generous to the labour element, because in that way they will not only be helping the labouring class as a whole but they will be helping themselves.
-Carried.

Well, there are some gentlemen in this House, Mr. Chairman, whose wisdom and intelligence is only capable of the expression "Carried;" they never did say anything else, and they cannot say anything else. Now, so far as the leader of the Opposition is concerned, I was one of those who advocated mercy last night, and I am advocating mercy now. Like my friend from Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) I wish it were possible for the Government to reconsider the stand that it has taken, but like my friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) last night, I may be at liberty to distinguish a little bit, although my philosophy may not be any more logical than. his. The leader of the Opposition said that we extended mercy last night, but that we are extending no mercy this evening. But although last night the leader of the Opposition and his followers held it a sin against women who were destroying our social life, to-night they will not hold it a sin against the men who attempted to destroy our national life. Let me point out another fact. Most of the employees recognize the relation of employer and employee so far as they and the Dominion Government are concerned, with this difference, that the relation is as to the whole of the Dominion and not as between individual employer and his employees alone. -So that the obligation upon the employee is greater in that respect. If it were not a fact that an attempt was made to usurp civil authority and to disrupt our national life, I would be prepared to say that the Government should be very lenient indeed in considering the case of the postal men. That is why I put the question to the Acting Minister of Justice, in order to satisfy myself that these men must have had notice, and I may say that if the movement which was set on foot had succeeded to any great extent the leader of the Opposition would not have had the opportunity to show mercy to anybody, and a Soviet Government might be sitting in this House to-day. Of course, the leader of the Opposition and my friends opposite may say that a Soviet Government would
be a good deal better than the one in office at the present time.
We do not go that far.	[DOT]

On section 1-unlawful associations:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This section is taken
practically word for word from the resolution concurred in by the House with regard to sedition. There will be one slight change; 1 purpose moving that the words " two justices of the peace " be changed to read " justice of the peace " in the second
4.356

line of subsection 6. I have been waited upon by certain members of the executive of the Police Association, and am convinced that if two justices of the peace are going to be necessary in every case, the proper working of this clause will be impracticable.

A stipendiary magistrate
has the power of two justices of the peace. Natutrally, he is a different sort of judicial officer from a justice of the peace.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but there are no stipendiary magistrates except at rather important points.
They go on circuit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh no.
They do in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They certainly do not
go on any circuit in our province.

I can quite see the
convenience of the change proposed by the minister, but I would hesitate to confide to one justice of the pe&ce, having regard to the way these officers are named in certain parts of the country, the extremely important and inquisitorial powers which are given under this section. I have heard, for instance, of men being appointed justices of the peace who were retired butchers and retired men of other walks of life which, though eminently respectable, did not tend to any knowledge of the law. It seems to me that the minister proposes to put rather strong powers in the hands of one justice of the peace.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Criminal Code
gives to justices of the peace in many cases powers of an equally important and far-reaching character. The power of arrest is vested in one justice of the peace. It is true they are not always lawyers or judges; they may be retired butchers or any other persons whom the provincial government considers to have common sense. Not very much harm has been done through rash action on the part of justices of the peace; where such a thing does occur, it is easily corrected. If the Act is to be efficient it is better to have one justice of the peace do this, because a man might have to travel thirty miles; it might even be out of the question to obtain justices of the peace.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I assume that the offences recognized and dealt with under this Act are all indictable offences and that they will be dealt with along the lines of procedure laid out for such offences?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the Act provides that a charge made under this Act shall be laid before the proper tribunal, I am not very much alarmed, because I have confidence in our courts. But I do not think that such a serious crime should be dealt with by an ordinary magistrate who cannot be expected to understand the real seriousness of the offence that he is trying. As to one magistrate having the power to issue a warrant, arrest a man, put him through his preliminary examination and send him up to the Supreme Court, it would seem to be as well to have one magistrate do that as two. But subsection 6 of this section seems to be somewhat different from the Code. According to the present criminal law, if information is laid against a man and he is arrested for any crime, and if there is reason to believe that certain evidence in the way of books or letters is available or obtainable, then the magistrate has the power to issue a search warrant, to impound such books and letters, and to take them into the custody of the court.
But that is always done after the man is arrested and in custody. I observe here that power is given, before anybody is arrested, to go in and seize such books. That is different from the ordinary procedure, and I should like the minister to consider the matter. When it is supposed that a crime has been committed by somebody and that there are some letters and books and other stuff that may prove the guilt, the stuff is taken with the person, but I have never heard of the stuff being taken first and the man afterward.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The usual procedure is that the information must be laid and sworn to, and after the information is laid charging the offence, then the search warrant issues, and that is the procedure here. The information must be laid charging the offence; it must charge some person with the offence, and that being done, the search warrant may issue if the application is sufficient to cover it. I do not see any variance from the prevailing principle of the Code. I move to amend clause 1 by striking out the words " two justices," in line 29 and in line 49 on page 2 of the Bill and replacing the said words by the word " justice."

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 2-carrying concealed weapons without a permit an offence-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
At the present time no one may carry a concealed weapon upon his person without a permit from a constable or other police authority, but it has been held in the courts that if a man carries it in his grip, for example, he is not carrying it on his person, and in that way the Act has been circumvented. This makes it an offence to carry it at all. Furthermore, it makes it an offence for a person to keep a concealed weapon in his home except upon license. The great difficulty that the police are confronted with to-day is the really alarming prevalence of revolvers and other weapons held by people in their homes ready for action at any time and conveyed from one to another without any control whatever being exercisable by the civil authorities. The police have waited upon the Department of Justice in this regard, and the Dominion police have strongly recommended that a system of license be established so that a man may get a license from any police authority in his neighbourhood, and tfiat license shall be good within the sphere of jurisdiction of that police authority. Otherwise, these weapons shall not be carried. My last words apply to aliens only; they do not apply to British subjects. The effect is that no one can carry a concealed weapon on his person or in a grip, or carry it about at all concealed, except with a license. That has been the law of the land, but it has been evaded by men putting weapons in their grips instead of on their persons. But an alien will not hereafter be able to have a revolver, firearms and so forth unless he gets a license. He must first procure a license, and that license shall be good within the area of the jurisdiction of the party giving the license. For instance, if be a provincial constable, the license shall be good within the jurisdiction of that constable, that is, within the province. If it is a city authority, that license will be good in that city. For example, in Montreal, these Weapons are sold, and they are conveyed from there to all parts of the country, and dangerous men have been found with these weapons in their possession-one, two, three and even four weapons, which, doubtless, would have been used had it not been for the surprise with which the men were taken. The police authorities brought very many such cases to my notice, and they say that the trouble can be controlled only by extending the license system to the home, where aliens are concerned. These men are not British subjects; they are very often alien enemies; they are sometimes not; but it is
no hardship on their part, if their reputation is good, to say to them: You must get a license from the police authorities of your neighbourhood before you are allowed to keep these weapons in your homes.

If the law is a good one, why should it not apply to British subjects as well as to aliens? Why make a distinction between aliens and people who are not aliens? Personally I do not like to see on our statute books anything which makes a distinction between an alien and a British subject.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The statute books are full of such distinctions.

Why should that be the
case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Have you not the alien
vote?

That is for the purpose of keeping the Government in power. I can understand the reason for that. But a British subject can do as much damage with a revolver as an alien, and personally I do not consider that every British subject you see is a paragon of excellence and every alien a dangerous character. The minister seems to go on the assumption of the Englishman who says:
" 'E's a stranger; let's 'eave 'arf a brick at 'im." The very fact that a man does not happen to have been born under the British flag does not of itself make that man a desperate character. If this law is to be put on the statute book, it should apply to all classes of citizens, aliens and British subjects.

speechtext:
During the last two

speechtext:
I am talking about the municipal authorities. The population of our penitentiaries and prisons is almost *5 per cent alien. I will give the figures in the jail at Guelph, the city in which I live.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am trying to treat the matter seriously, and I am giving some strong facts regarding the question, and it is for these reasons that I have thought it necessary to insert a new clause so as to control the use of firearms and other dangerous weapons by aliens.

Subclause 1 of clause 2
says:
(1) Paragraph (a) of subsection one of section one hundred and eighteen of the Criminal Code, chapter one hundred and forty-six of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1906, as enacted toy chapter thirteen of the statutes of 1913 is amended by inserting after the word " person " in the first line thereof the words " or is carrying concealed."

speechtext:
The clause as amended will provide that every one will be guilty of an offence who has upon his >
person, " Of is carrying " a pistol, etc. At a recent assize at Yorkton, Saskatchewan, there was a list of seventeen offences all of a major character, ranging from murder, through many cases of manslaughter, indecent assault, rape, etc., and only one of the offenders was other than alien.

speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) would be able to say, but I would be surprised if the British citizens were not in the majority.

I oppose the idea that there should be one law for the alien and one law for the British subject. Of course, it is apparent that on questions of voting or office-holding there must be a difference, but .in regard to police ^matters and the keeping of the peace I think it is unwise to lay down a double rule. I quite sympathize with the proposal to compel all those who have lethal weapons to obtain a permit. It may be true that our alien population has been more free in the use of these weapons than people of British blood or British citizenship, and I think the habit 
of carrying weapons on the person or concealing them in the home should be restrained in all classes. It has been the glory of [British countries wherever the British flag floats that underneath its folds all those who conduct themselves peacefully are treated in the same manner, and I would ask the minister to make the obligation to obtain a permit apply not only to aliens but to all subjects. On the whole, the practice of carrying and concealing weapons is to be deprecated. It is far better for people who are afraid of being burglarized, as the newspapers say, to rely on the police force for protection rather than to attempt their own protection by the use of pistols, which are a source of danger to children. I seriously submit to ti,e minister the undesirability of having dual regulations applying to aliens and British subjects.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman knew what those who have to do with law and order know, he would not have very much hesitation about enacting this legislation. To compel every one to obtain a permit would be a very burdensome matter, indeed. It is burdensome enough to compel all aliens to have a permit, and I do not want to tax the administration of justice more than is necessary. The information at hand is enough to convince any one that it is high time we saw to it that weapons were not being concealed, not by tens or scores, or even hundreds, but by thousands, upon thousands of people in this country, nearly all aliens, only a very small percentage of them being British subjects. The hon. gentleman thinks it is unBritish to distinguish between aliens and British people, but it is not so. There is scarcely a line of our statutes that does not make the distinction. Under our Dominion Lands Act-enacted, I think, by hon. gentlemen opposite-aliens -cannot take Dominion lands. Aliens- cannot get a patent. They are subject to deportation, while British subjects are not-and the distinction is made all down the line.
I thought that a law was promoted the other day in the House providing that British subjects should be deported if they were undesirable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is a certain class of British subjects to whom we have extended the law heretofore applicable to aliens

those bom outside- of Canada. We have, under the stress of exceptional circumstances, seen fit to enact that law. But throughout the statutes the distinction be-

tween aliens and British subjects has been drawn, and it is juist as much British as it is a matter of common sense. This measure is founded on necessity and is dictated in view of circumstances that exist.

I was at pains to state in my remarks that I had no objection to the safeguarding of the public interests by forcing aliens to obtain permits to have weapons in their houses.. I said I was sympathetic as regards that, and the minister inferred that I was not, and therefore I think his argument was unfair in that respect.. I say that it is a mistaken policy and one contrary to British traditions to have a certain set of police regulations for aliens and another set for citizens. We should not have these deferentiations except where necessary. Of course they are necessary in the case of voting and in the taking up of land. But they are surely not necessary in regard to the observing of order and good government in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is the question.

As my hon. friend sitting next to me (Mr. Jacobs) suggests, all aliens are not desperate characters. would be obliged to obtain a permit to have a revolver in his possession, whilst a denizen of the purlieus of London or Glasgow' who happens to be a British subject w'ould not be obliged to obtain it if he came here. Do I understand that is to be the Tule?

Every man who comes to this country seeks to become a British citizen; else, why should he come to this country? Do I understand that so soon as that person sheds- his alien citizenship and becomes a British subject, or as soon as- the Secretary of State, under the new law, immerses him in the official baptismal font, he, ipso- facto, is permitted to carry a weapon?-that this is one of the rights of British citizenship?

speechtext:
He cannot carry a
weapon, but he can have it in his home.
He can have it in his house in the same way as he would have a bottle of Scotch whisky in his cellar?

The city of Stratford, in . the county that I have the honour to represent, has sent to the Government a petition based upon evils that have arisen through aliens in that district. My hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) says fhat such petitions have come in and that the police records, show' the desirability of the law. Notwithstanding that, gentlemen on the opposite side of the House, whenever anything comes up between the Britisher and the alien, press the alien to their hearts with the greatest gusto and glee, even though it goes to the extent of making a point against a Britisher- 1
That is incorrect.
Mr. Chairman-
Order.
The hon. gentleman may disavow it, but I am placing what I say is the real, honest interpretation on their attitude not only in the-
It is a dishonest interpretation.

They seem to be perfectly delighted when they are ragging the Brit-

isher. There seems to be the same complaint by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and those on the other side of the House who think like him. The Britisher has never been a man who, in his own environment, has been accustomed to carrying concealed weapons. We find many people from southern nations especially who, as a matter of environment, are brought up to the habit of carrying weapons. Without being offensive I may say that the Italian is noted for his dirk and stiletto. It cjoes seem to me that for the public good this is wise legislation. I would go farther and amend the Immigration Act to the extent that if an alien came to this country and was found with a concealed weapon upon his person he would be refused entry and sent back till he learned better.
That was made the law this session.

These hon. gentlemen will defend the man who comes in here with a dagger in the back of his belt or in his shoe, while they will not defend the Britisher who, as is well known throughout the world, loves a standup fight, square and fair, with his fists. Are we to allow these aliens to bring their bad habits, notions and vicious practices into this country? Will these hon. gentlemen come out and meet that situation at all ? In spite of what the police records show and the knowledge possessed by the Government, will these hon. gentlemen insist on permitting aliens to come in here with weapons?
I must protest against such an argument as that.
Order.

The hon. member (Mr. McMaster) is always, as I said before, willing to protest against anything that really discloses the effect of his own propaganda. He does not mind having aliens in Canada with concealed weapons and assumes that they do not carry them. He has not the slightest sympathy with the Britisher because he depends on his pair of fists in a manly way, so long as the alien may be permitted to stand, under the law, in a superior position and be allowed to carry-weapons. That is the inverse of the argument that he uses. This is not the first time that we have found the hon. gentleman championing the cause of the aliens; it shows in the attitude of the hon. gentleman, and he takes up the alien's cause whenever he gets a chance. This Bill, to

my mind, is one of the most important that has been brought into this Parliament for many years. It is a Bill especially for the public good, and for the protection of the alien who is good as against the bad alien, and of the British people in this country. In the Solicitor General's town alone, in the last two years, there have been at least a dozen tragedies in which aliens took part, arising largely out of the habit which they have of carrying concealed weapons. There has been mystery after mystery all through Western Ontario traceable to aliens and difficult to solve. If a law is put into force to stop the practice on the part of aliens of carrying concealed weapons the public will feel safe in their homes and there will be further protection given to life and property.
Mr. iMoMA'STER: I just want to register an emphatic protest against the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy). He has said that I was here to defend aliens in their wrong-doing. I respectfully and emphatically deny that, and I say that such a statement is unfair and unjust.
And untrue.

Of course it is untrue. I hate to take up the time of the committee. I can merely repeat what I said before. I am in favour of legislation to control the carrying of concealed weapons, but I say it should apply not only to aliens, but to all citizens.

I want to protest also against the insinuations made by the hon. member (Mr. Morphy), Tvhen he says that the remarks made by the hon. member for Brome are in line with what the Opposition say. I take issue with him and I say that he is not only unjust in his language, but that his statement is absolutely incorrect. Take the case of a decent citizen from the United States, who is as good as any British subject who ever trod upon British soil; he comes here, and because his child has an air gun in the house, he has to trot out and get a permit, and if he does not he is liable to a fine. I do not say that I am against this legislation; on the contrary-.but because I say it works a hardship and because I call the attention of the committee to that fact, the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) gets up and says we are pro-enemy in principle and un-Britisln That kind of thing is played out. Whenever we pass criminal or civil legislation, or any other

kind of legislation, the hon. member for North Perth, who is generally pretty fair outside of this House, seems to forget himself the moment he begins to speak. He wants to put himself on record in Hansard as being a patriot and he wants to put us on record in Hansard as being the worst enemies of the country. I am surprised that he does not move that beside every member on this side of the House a Dominion policeman should be placed to keep him from blowing up the building. I do not intend to take any more of this kind of bluff or this talk about waving the flag and winning the war while hiding sins of all sorts under the guise of patriotism. It is about time that sort of thing came to an end. Let us have done with that kind of business.

I was not aware that I had even waved the flag or mentioned the war in my remarks. However, if the hon. gentleman has taken that meaning out of anything I said, I will leave it to himself to justify his words, nothing from me in the nature of an answer is required. I pointed out, even speaking of the American citizen as an alien, it is well known that the practice has prevailed in the United States, particularly in the south, of carrying a revolver as a matter of habit. Consequently, that particular citizen coming in here might follow his habit of carrrying a revolver, and that habit has some significance. The man who carries a revolver concealed has got it for destructive purposes.
That is not the section that is in question. This section deals with, for example, an air-gun..

The section is not really aimed at air-guns that are harmless.' However, air-guns have been used throughout the United States with the most deadly effect by criminals of the worst class who killed their man through the medium of an air-gun-as deadly a weapon as a powder-charged gun-and escaped the penalty by virtue of no alarm as a result of the concussion having rung out on the air. I think the provision is a good one and should go through.

The hon. member seems to think we are here for the purpose of defending the undesirable alien. We are not here for that purpose but to defend the desirable alien. I think it will be admitted generally in this House that the desirable alien is vastly in the majority in this country to the undesirable alien and
he must be protected from hysterical legislation which we have been putting on the statute 'books for the last year or two. There seems to be no end to the lengths to which the Government will go in the matter of legislating against citizens who have been invited to come and live in this country. As soon as they come here they have the same rights, and the same privileges, and they should be put under the same obligation, as people who are natives of Canada, British subjects, and have resided here all their lives. There should not be a different law for one class as against another. We know that by the old system under the Roman Empire and the early republic, there was a law for the stranger and there was a law for the Roman citizen. Now we are going back to that system, we are oblivious of what has taken place in the last two thousand years, and we are legislating to-day in the Parliament of Canada in the same way that the Roman barbarians did. These aliens must have some protection within reasonable limits.' If they are undesirable, deport them from the country. If they carry concealed weapons and are a danger to peaceful citizens living in the community, why not give municipalities the power to issue permits to these people, and have them amend the municipal regulations in that regard, and not amend the criminal law in order to strike at the very foundations of the liberties of a very large number of people in this country. We have tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of people in this country who are not yet naturalized, and under the Naturalization Act which has been just put through, it will be many years before they can get naturalization, and while they are in this stage,, suspended between heaven and earth, they are to be put to no end of inconvenience, for no other reason than that they do not happen to be born in the country. I say it is a slur upon tens of thousands of respectable citizens in Canada to put upon the statute books a law of this kind simply because a handful of people in certain parts of the country have not behaved themselves. If they are undesirable, deport them,-the Minister of Immigration has the power, under the new law to deport undesirables,-but I would make a plea for the respectable alien, and ask that this law do not pass.

On section 15

Crown's right to challenge when jurors stood by are recalled:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The rule now is that
the Crown can tell a juror to stand aside; then when the panel is exhausted the jurors are recalled in the order in which they stood aside. . What is the meaning of this . section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has been held in a case decided in British Columbia, the King vs. Churton, that where the Crown orders members of the jury panel, when called, to stand aside, and then the panel is exhausted and there is not a jury secured, the jurymen who have been ordered to stand aside cannot again be challenged by the Crown unless the Crown is prepared to show cause as well. That is to say, the burden is on the Crown not only to challenge, but also to show cause before any member of the panel who has stood aside can be called as a juror. Though the Crown may not have exhausted its right of challenge, it can no more exercise that right after the challenge is exhausted unless it is prepared to show cause. That never was the intention of the Act, but because the word " and " is used there instead of "or," that is held to be the meaning; and it appears to me that the court of British Columbia were undoubtedly right in their finding. The idea is, 'by changing the word " and" to " or," to enable the Crown, if it has not exhausted its right of challenge when the jury is empanelled ot continue to challenge until its right is exhausted, and thereafter, and thereafter alone, to show cause.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It will not have the effect of extending the power of challenge?
