speechtext: No.

I suggest to my hon. friend, in connection with this Bill, an amendment for next session if he has to deal with the Criminal Code. As my hon-. friend is aware, in the province of Quebec, in any trial by jury the accused is entitled to a jury de medietate linguae. If he is French, he may ask that his jury be composed of six jurors of the French language and six of English language, and if he is English, vice versa. This custom was established during the early days of British domination in Canada. According to the constitutional documents the principle was admitted in order to placate the then English speaking minority. As my hon. friend is aware-and I do not wish to raise any religious question in connection with this suggested amendment-at the time of the cession of this country to France the Blue

Laws, as they are generally known, were in existence in Great Britain and in almost every British colony-with the exception, however, of the province of Quebec, which then comprised the whole of Canada as if-then existed. When Governor Murray took hold of the colony on behalf of His Majesty ' the King, he issued an ordinance in 1764 in which it was stipulated that "in all trials in this court, all His Majesty's subjects in the colony are to be admitted on juries without distinction." The English-speaking subjects of the King resented the treatment of the new subjects of His Majesty, the French, who had just been conquered, on a footing of equality with them as regards the jury system, and made representations to the British authorities.
In a memorandum addressed to His Majesty on the 16th October, 1764, they complain bitterly of the fact-and I am using the exact words which they then used:
-that persons professing the religion of the Church of Rome have heen impannelled on grand and petty juries even where two Protestants were parties.
In the same memorandum they recall the fact that by an Act of William III, chapter 5, section 8, "No Papist shall practise the common law as chancellor, clerk, attorney or solicitor, etc.," and they conclude their memorandum by stating:
We, therefore, believe that the admitting of
persons of the Roman religion	as
jurors is an open violation of our most sacred laws and liberties and tending to the utter subversion of the Protestant religion and His Majesty's power, authority, right and possession of the province to which we belong.
My hon. friend will find this memorandum at page 154 of Constitutional Documents published by Shortt & Doughty.
I recall this just to point out the origin, of the jury de medietate linguae. This memorandum was examined by the law officers of Great Britain, and the decision given was that the new subjects of His Majesty could serve as jurors, and in 1776, on the 1st July, a new ordinance was issued declaring that, in all actions "between British-born subjects and Canadians"-it will be noticed that in those days there was no such distinction as English-Canadians and French-Canadians amongst the old inhabitants of the colonies-" the juries are to be composed of an equal number of each, if it be required by either of the parties." This is from Shortt and Doughty, Constitutional Documents, page 173. This is the origin of the mixed jury as we have it in the province of Quebec in all jury cases,

be they civil or criminal. But I wish to qualify this statement by adding that it was at the urgent and earnest request of the British minority then that this institution of the mixed jury was established. This principle, which was crystallized in this ordinance which I have just quoted, was later on, after the union of the two provinces of Upper and Lower Canada, reproduced fn our statute, and it is now the law of the land; and I think we have in the Criminal Code one clause which deals with the jury de medietate linguae in the province of Quebec.
The reason why I gave this short history of the jury de medietate linguae is this. Whilst this principle is admitted in our province, yet it has been found in some cases that the proceedings taking place before such juries de medietate linguae were conducted only in one language. In ordinary cases I would not take a strong exception because generally the judge and the Crown prosecutor and the attorney for the defence will see that the rights of the accused are duly protected. But what I wish to- draw especially to the attention of the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), and where I should like to see him introduce an amendment to the Criminal Code with regard to the jury de medietate linguae in our province is in capital cases. I have in mind a -case which was heard in one of the districts not too far from Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Veuillette case?

Yes, it was a murder case. The young man, a mere child who. I think, was not twenty years old, was accused of murder -and was sentenced as a murderer. A jury de medietate linguae was selected, and the whole of the evidence was given in the English language. My contention is' that the evidence should be translated in French, that is, all the proceedings in those capital oases should, when there is a jury de medietate linguae, be conducted in both languages. I expressly state the capital cases, because in such cases no chances whatsoever should be taken as to the manner in which the evidence is presented to the jury. The six English-speaking jurors and the six Frenchspeaking jurors should have an equal opportunity of hearing the evidence in their language. The addresses of counsel should be in both languages, and especially should the charge of the presiding judge be made in both languages. I have read the appeal .case as it was presented before the Supreme

Court, and it seems to me that there is a doubt in favour of the accused, and furthermore, four of the jurors gave affidavits after the trial that they had not understood certain phases of the evidence given during the trial. I do not, of course, wish to Te-open the trial; the case has been heard in the Supreme Court and unfortunately this young man has been executed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Hlis sentence was commuted, at all events, to prison for life.

I thought he had been executed, and I am very pleased to hear that his sentence has been commuted. My hon. friend must have taken into consideration the favourable circumstance which came out at the time the appeal was brought before the Supreme Court in that capital case, in that the prisoner had not received the full benefit of the proceedings as they should have been conducted. I rfrould ask my hon. friend during the recess to consider this case, which I presume he must have read since he commuted the sentence, and to amend the law next year so that in capital cases especially the evidence and proceedings of the court, and the charge of the judge, should be given in both languages in order to avoid any possibility of errors. Reading over that case to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago, I am under the impression that a serious error was made, because four of the jurors made affidavits declaring that they had not understood the whole of the evidence. I submit that this is a special privilege enjoyed by both races in the province of Quebec, and it dates as far hack as the early days of British domination. It was at the request of the English-speaking minority that the officers of the Crown in England granted that privilege, and in so far as it exists and is crystallized in our statute-book, there should be no question that the privilege should be exercised in the proper way. I ask my friend to kindly consider this question during the recess and make the necessary amendments if he thinks they should be made.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will not likely be the minister who will have consideration of the amendments to the Code for next session. The case which the hon. gentleman specifically brings to my attention, however, is one which, although it occurred some time ago, I have a very distinct and detailed recollection of. Veuillette had been sentenced to be hanged. He had been entitled to and had secured a jury composed half of English and half of French, and the trial

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: was conducted- wholly in English without any objection on the part of the defence, and, so far as appears in the record, to the understanding of the jurors and of the accused. After the sentence was passed and after the case came before the Department of Justice for consideration, the defence took an appeal to the Court of Appeal of the province of Quebec on the ground that the accused was entitled not only to a jury composed as it was, but to the trial being conducted in French as well as in English. In the Court of Appeal of Quebec it was held, Chief Justice Lamothe dissenting-I think I am right?-
Yes, that is right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
-that the accused would not be so entitled as his right. The -Chief Justice took the view that he was so entitled and that there should be a new trial. From the decision in that court appeal was taken to the Supreme Court of -Canada, where the view taken by Chief Justice Lamothe in the Court of Appeal below was upheld by Mr. Justice Brodeur but dissented from on the part of the other justices. On the part of Mr. Justice Anglin the dissent only took this ground, that although there was an irregularity in the conduct of the trial, in that the proceedings were not -coilducted in- both languages, that irregularity did not constitute a miscarriage of substantial justice, an-d that on that account, under the wording of the -section of the code, there- was no ground for reversing the verdict or ordering a new trial. I think the majority of the Supreme Court held that there was no irregularity in the conduct of the case in one language, although Mr. Justice Anglin- gave a strong judgment the other way, holding that there was an irregularity, but with the reservation that it did not go to the undoing of justice. Consequently, he concurred with the majority in refusing to reserve the case and upholding the verdict of the Court of Appeal of Quebec. When the case came before the Governor General for decision as to commutation-, that fact was before us. I do not think I am at liberty to say what was taken into account, but that fact was before us; and there was the further fact that the boy had come twice under the shadow of the gallo-ws and execution had been- postponed while indeed the gallows were erected outside his window. There was also the fact of his tender years and his near approach to immaturity o-f intellect. However, it is clear to all that if no substantial injustice occurs, then unEDITION

doubtedly the failure to conduct the trial in the two languages cannot be very serious. So long as all understand the proceedings there can be no substantial injustice, and I think that all must have understood the proceedings in this case, because I know that all the judges, except possibly Mr. Justice Brodeur, agreed that they were understood. I do not think the hon. member can be correct in regard to the four jurors taking the affidavit. So long as all understand the proceedings, under the law as it stands to-day there is no necessity for conducting the case in both languages. I do not think I need go further at the present time.

My hon. friend has made a fair statement of the case, and I may simply add that counsel whc represented the accused was a very young man who, in his factum before the Supreme .Court, made the statement that he was a very young member of the bar and had not then the advantages of the experience which he had since acquired, and that he was led into error, following the action of crown counsel and the presiding judge. As a matter of fact, my hon. friend will find in the record the affidavits of four jurors who declared that some portion of the evidence had not been fully understood by them. My hon. friend will understand that there would be less danger of miscarriage of justice if an amendment were introduced into the Criminal Code. It might be made applicable only to criminal cases, because I would rely on the common sense and good judgment of the court in other oases. In capital cases, however, no risk should be taken, and from time immemorial under the British law an accused has never been sentenced on a plea of guilty. The court will always order, in spite of his plea of guilty, that he be represented by counsel and that a case be made out. So that in capital cases where there is a jury de medietate linguae, it seems to me that as a matter of course the proceedings should be conducted in both languages,-the evidence, the addresses of counsel both for the Crown and for the defence, and especially the charge of the presiding judge. I am very glad that my hon. friend has a knowledge of this case, and I hope that with his fair sense of justice, during recess if he does not himself prepare an amendment, at least he will pave the way for his colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and endeavour to see that an amendment is introduced next session.

On section 14-prisoner must re-elect forty days before jury trials commence, or, if committed in that period, ten days before:

The amendment to section 14 provides that:
no (prisoner shall have a right to re-elect later than forty days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the court at (which trials (by jury can be had and if the prisoner was committed for trial within such forty days then not later than ten days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the court at which trials by jury can be had.
The effect of that will be that if a man is committed for trial within forty-one or forty-two days of the date fixed for the trial, he will only have forty-eight hours to elect. In many of the counties, if a man were committed in an outlying district, it would be impossible for him to come to the courthouse and elect before the forty days Bad expired. It would remove the right of election, and I would therefore beg to move that all the words after the word "had" in the fourth line be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

unless the prisoner was committed for trial within fifty days before the said date, in which event he must re-elect not later than ten days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the court at which trials by jury can (be had.

I was not here when the law was first passed. I would like to know the reason for this change. It seems to me that it will entail many trials by jury. As the law is at present the prisoner can elect at any time before the day appointed for the sittings of the court.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

On section 1	(97(b)-publishing, etc.,
seditious books, etc. (Reconsidered):

The amendment proposed by section 97 (b) in the second part of clause 1 makes it an offence for any person to publish, distribute or import any book, pamphlet, etc., promulgating the doctrines prohibited by section (97a). I can quite understand that it is necessary, if convictions are to be secured under this clause that there should be a presumption of knowledge, but it seems to me to be radically unfair that if a person is in a position to prove that he either printed, distributed, or imported any of this objectionable literature without having any knowledge of its contents, he should not be exonerated from responsibility or should be considered as a criminal. I would therefore, to put the argument shortly, like to suggest to the minister that to the clause there should be added a provision that no conviction should be recorded under subsection 1, 2 and 3 of clause 97 (b) if the prisoner satisfies the court that he had no knowledge that the literature contained the objectionable matter in reference to that he was charged with printing, distributing or importing. It strikes one as radically unfair that if perchance a printer printed a part of a work, the full import of which he did not understand, or somebody distributed a book the contents of which he did not know or, if somebody brought into the country a magazine without knowing the contents of it, he should stand trial and be convicted without having an opportunity of being freed under the charge if he satisfied the court that he had no knowledge of what the document contained and was really innocent in the eyes of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not disposed to favour the suggestion although I would like to hear some discussion upon it. I fear that if the suggestion is accepted it is going to defeat the law.
How does the law read now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no law; 97 (b) is new.
I mean this proposed law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It reads as follows:
97b. (1) Any person who prints, publishes, bdits, issues, circulates, sells, or offers for sale or distribution any book, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, paper, circular, card, letter, writing, print, publication or document of any kind, in which is taught, advocated, advised or defended, or who shall in any manner teach, advocate, or advise or defend the use, without
277 i
authority of law, of force, violence, terrorism, or physical injury to person or property, or threats of such injury, as a means of accomplishing any governmental, industrial or economic change, or otherwise, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for not less than one year, and not more than twenty years.
(2)	Any person who circulates or attempts to circulate or distribute any book, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, paper, circular, card, letter, writing, print, publication, or document of any kind, as described in this section by mailing the same or causing the same to ibe mailed or posted in any Port Office, letter box, or other mail receptacle in Canada, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall be liable to imprisonment for not less than one year and not more than twenty years.
(3)	Any person who imports into Canada from any other country, or attempts to import by or through any means whatsoever, any book, newspaper, periodical, pamphlet, picture, paper, circular, oard, letter, writing, print, publication or document of any kind as described in this section, shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for not less than one year and not more than twenty years.
My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) suggests that no person who does this shall be convicted if he is able to show that he did not know that the contents of the literature were of this character. What I say is that I fear that an amendment of that sort would go a long way, in practical operation, to- defeat the purpose of the law because, these men who -bring in, print and circulate this stuff, or are responsible for it, would have very few qualms of conscience about getting up and saying that they did not know that its contents were of this character and that' they had heard that it was very good literature. In that way they would completely escape responsibility. The man who brings in or prints literature must take the responsibility for the character of that literature and we must not allow him to escape under any plea of lack of knowledge.
I do not know that I would go that far. I think I would be willing to use the word "knowingly." It is an old principle that there must be guilty knowledge.

Of course, I cannot enforce my view on the minister, and I must bow to his judgment, but I cannot bring myself to agree with the principle that if a man happens to send to the United States and buy a pamphlet or a book even though he should prove that he knew nothing whatever about the contents of the book that he had brought into Canada for his private reading, he should be treated as criminal. Or if some person came into a oity and asked a certain man to distribute certain

literature from house to house-that is the ordinary bill poster or distributor to be found in many of our cities.-that he should be held to be a criminal simply because he entered into a contractural relationship, though he demonstrated beyond the shadow of a doubt that he was not in any way endeavouring to break the law. Of course, if the principle is to secure a conviction at any cost then probably this legislation will do it. But-I have always been moved by the idea that it was wise that the benefit of the doubt should be given, and that it was better at times that those who had broken the law should be acquitted rather than that those who were innocent should be convicted, because the stigma of a criminal character is not k pleasant thing for a man to carry through life. I cannot bring myself, therefore, to agree with the reasoning of the minister, although of necessity I bow to his judgment.
Mr, McKENZIE: I wish to say to the minister on this point, and I have said it so often in this House that I am almost getting tired of it, that there must be a criminal mind before there can be a crime. It is also implied anyhow that the man does a thing knowing it to be wrong. I think we can always trust to the jury and to the judge to believe or disbelieve the accused person's plea- of not knowing. Of course, although it is provided for in the law the man may say " I did not know anything about it," but it is for the jury to believe him or not. If the judge says "you did know, you could not help knowing," and advises the jury that under the circumstances the man could not help knowing, that he was familiar with this book, and with its contents, and if the jury believe the accused did know, of course they would bring him in guilty. But I think the proper way to legislate jn a criminal matter is that if a man knowingly does a thing he is guilty, and it is for the jury to believe or not believe his plea that he did not know.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: House again in Committee on the proposed resolutions with regard to judges' salaries, (resumed from Saturday, June 28). Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think it is a little
too late to take up these resolutions, but if there is anything of a brief nature the minister desires to bring forward we can go on with it.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The discussion on this matter need only be very brief, because even the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) says his mind is so fully persuaded.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not see him here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps that is why
he is not here.

I am here all right, and I take exception to what the minister has said. I am not convinced in this matter,
I am far from being so but I do not want to take up any more time with any extended remarks, because I see it is useless. However, I want to register my protest because the equalization of the salaries of the judges of the province of Quebec has not been touched. I am not going to call attention to any specific instance, but I , will say this:	Heretofore, when we have
asked for the equalization of the salaries of the judges of Quebec, the answer given to us by hon. gentlemen opposite is that if they opened up the question of judges' salaries in one province they would need to open up the same question throughout the whole Dominion. Or to put it another way, if the question of salaries of judges throughout the whole Dominion were not opened up, it would give rise to discontent, and the Government would be flooded with demands. Every province in the Dominion to-day sees the salaries of its judges increased except the province of Quebec; that is the one province in which the judges' salaries are not touched. Hereafter if ever the question is again opened up, I do not want the argument to'be advanced that you cannot touch the salaries of the judges of one province without dealing with the salaries of judges in all the other provinces. I think a fair method would be to reverse that argument and say " You cannot deal with the salaries of judges in all the other provinces and leave the salaries in one province altogether untouched." The acting minister has given us as a reason that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) himself is from the province of Quebec, and that he knows best what should be done. I refuse to accept that reason. It would be very easy to either hold this legislation back until the minister's return', or to communicate with him and ascertain his views on the subject. I repeat, it is of no use trying to get justice in this matter, but I serve notice that perhaps in two or three years when we on this side will be in office, we will open the case for the province of

Quebec, and I do not want the other provinces to be taken by surprise if we close the case to them.

Before the resolution is finally passed, I wish to make an appeal on behalf of Mr. Justice Weir whose case is altogether exceptional, and one which I know will appeal to the Acting Minister of Justice. Mr. Justice Weir is the judge for the district of Pontiac, a rural district, and he also renders efficient and almost continuous service in the district of Montreal. All the other rural judges who render the same service in the district of Montreal are given $7,000 a year, while Mr. Justice Weir is left at $5,000. The principle of equal pay for equal work should certainly apply to all the judges of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec. Therefore, I bring this matter again to the attention of the Acting Minister of Justice- 1 believe his notice was called to it on a previous occasion-and I ask him now to consider it in a spirit of fairness and to do justice to this judge. It is not fair to Mr. Justice Weir, doing exactly the same work as the other judges are doing, both in their rural districts and the city of Montreal, that he should be receiving $2,000 a year less than they.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not want the hon. gentleman (Mr. McMaster) to conclude that because I do not feel like amending these regulations I am passing any judgment at all upon his appeal on behalf of Mr. Justice Weir. I feel that the resolutions are not intended at all to take care of what I might call the domestic inequalities of a province.
. They are intended merely to take care of the general insufficiency of salaries of judges of the lower courts. That is the primary purpose of the resolutions. They have a secondary purpose, and that is to raise the salaries of Superior Courts in outside provinces to an equality with the salaries of these courts in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, but in no way now to go into any province and charge the relationships of judges, or to attempt to bring equality of salary where there is equality of labour and of service in that province. If I attempted that I would have to go into many other provinces besides Quebec, but Quebec would be the last that I would enter because as acting minister, when the minister himself is from that province, it seemed to me very becoming on my part to leave such decision for one so much better qualified to judge. It is on that
plea that I ask that this appeal be not pressed in relation to these resolutions.
As for the claim of the member from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), whose attitude to-night I appreciate very much, I do not remember its ever being argued-perhaps it was-that one cannot touch the salaries of the judges in one province without touching them in another province. I will never argue that. Wherever it can be shown that in fairness the salaries of the judges of any one province should be raised, then, that claim should stand on its own merits alone. That attitude I take now, and I will undertake to take it in future.

I want to call attention to the fact that the province of Prince Edward Island has been discriminated against in this Bill. I notice that the chief justice of Prince Edward Island, who now receives $6,000 a year, is to be increased $500, and the puisne judges who receive only $5,200, are to be increased $300 each. That make a difference against our judges of $1,500. I know those judges. They attend chambers every day, they work faithfully, and they are men of good abilities; and I do not see why they should be discriminated against. To my mind it is very unfair, and I would like to know if the old excuse is advanced of cheaper living down there, which to my mind is no excuse at all. It is true we have not a large population. We might give a very good reason why it it not large-it is on account .of the policy pursued ever since we joined Confederation -the terms of our joining not having been carried out. However, I would suggests as a compromise that each judge of Prince Edward Island should receive an additional $1,000 to his salary, although even at that our judges would not be receiving as much as the judges of the other provinces by $1,000. I repeat, I strongly protest against the discrimination that is now proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. member was not present at the last meeting of the Committee when I placed this matter in the light that I conceive is just. It is true there is a difference between the salaries of the higher court judges in the Island and those of the higher court judges in the other provinces. That was not based on the principle that living is cheaper in the Island. If that had been the principle, then I would have made the salaries of the County Court judges in the Island lower than those of the County Court judges in the other provinces, but they are made exactly the same.

I did not conceive that the salaries of the judges of the higher courts needed to be increased at all on the score of the cost of living. They were sufficient everywhere to take care of the cost of living; that is to say, not ostentatiously to take care of it, but in a reasonable way. It was rather based upon the principle that the duties and responsibilities of a chief justice or a judge of the higher courts in the province of Prince Edward Island were not at all equal to those of a judge of the higher courts in the provinces of Ontario or Quebec, or, indeed, of any other province. That principle has been in effect ever since Confederation, and, so far as I know, has not been controverted-at all events, it has never been upset. , It is argued that the difference is now greater. That is not the case. The difference is a little greater as between Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia being now $1,500 where it was $1,000, but the difference is less as between Prince Edward Island and Quebec or Ontario, where the difference was formerly $2,000, but is now only $1,500. So that as compared with the rest of Canada the difference is just about the same as it has always been. It is hardly fair for the hon. member for Queen's, P.E.I. (Mr. Nicholson), to charge that his province is discriminated against in the matter of judicial salaries, because a reference to the figures will show that of all the nine provinces of Confederation Prince Edward Island obtains a larger allowance proportionately to population than any other province, the next largest being the province of Quebec. I am sorry that the two provinces with the largest amount per capita are the two that are complaining against the Bill. The allowance for Prince Edward Island amounts to about 30 cents per capita, while Quebec comes next with an allowance of about 17 cents per capita. So Prince Edward Island has almost double the per capita for judicial salaries compared with the next highest, that of Quebec.
What about the Yukon?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Yukon is not a province. It is true that the cost of salaries in the Yukon is $5,000, or nearly a dollar a head, but that is very different from the Island. I think it is only right that the Island should have the highest cost per capita, because where you have the lowest population, other things being equal, you are going to have the highest cost per capita of judicial salaries. But it is so very much the highest that I do not think it is fair to

say the Island is discriminated against. I am just maintaining the proportion that has always been maintained, which seems to me to be just in this regard, and which, indeed, is recognized in other spheres as well as that of judicial salaries.

I see there is a Bill on
the Order Paper to amend the Judges Act, which Bill was passed by the Senate. I understand that that Bill deals with some provisions of the Judges Act with regard to retiring allowances and the rate of pay for judges doing work outside their judicial duties. Is it the intention of the minister to press that Bill in this House?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is no Bill of mine. I am not only not pressing it, but I shall not allow it to go through in its present form if I can help it.
It has passed the Senate.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think if my hon.
friend will discuss the Bill with the hon. member for Maisonneuve he will change his demeanour.

I reiterate the objections I expressed the other day to increasing the salaries of the judges of the superior courts without revising the provisions of the Judges Act with reference to retiring allowances. I think we should cut off the retiring allowance of judges after fifteen years' service on the Bench.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
These resolutions do
that, unless in cases where the Governor in Council determines it is in the public interest to allow them, -which cases would be, I presume, oases of illness or unfitness for office.

I objected to that provision the other day. I do not like to see that discretion put in the hands of the Gov-, emor in Council, which in practice is the Government, because it is then subject to political influence. Sometimes it is desired to get a person out of the way to make place for another person, or a person wants to get off the Bench to go into political life. We have seen that in the past. A judge was allowed to retire, and not long afterwards he was a candidate at the general election.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Government cannot put a judge off the Bench.
I mean a judge may want to 'be superannuated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would not be subject to political influence.

I mean he could exercise political influence -with the Government. He might be a friend of the Government, and they might not like to refuse to consent to his retirement, but, on the contrary, might desire to facilitate it to afford a vacancy for another of their friends.
I believe that this provision should not be enacted. A judge should be allowed to retire only when incapacitated for the performance of his duties on account of old age or illness. Before we increase the salaries, we should revise the retiring allowance provisions of the Judges Act. Is it *still the intention of the minister to make provision in the Bill for subjecting the salaries of judges to the federal income tax?

Has the minister considered the advisability of extending the application of the principle of paying judges in proportion to the amount of judicial service which they render? I understand that that move has been made in Hamilton, Toronto, London, and, I think, Ottawa. I think I can safely say that the county court judge in my county does1 more work during the year than the judges in many counties put together. If the principle is recognized of paying larger salaries to judges in the larger places because , of the greater amount of work which they do, then that principle should apply down the line so that in counties such as I speak of the judges will get salaries commensurate with the services they perform.
Mr, MEIGHEN: I have not considered that, except in the 'Sense that I will refer to in a minute. If one were to attempt to make a sliding scale of salaries based upon the amount of work done in particular counties, I am afraid that judges or friends of judges would make the continuance of such a system almost impossible. Daily, hourly, I do not know how often, pressure would be exerted by various local communities and by friends of members of the Bench with a view to having judges placed in a higher rank, and that pressure would be yielded to until we would have the condition of affairs that we have now in the province of Quebec, where the demand is made that all the judges be put in the highest rank with the least possible delay. I know that the burden of the work varies greatly, but I think the remedy is rather along the line of distributing the burden more evenly. I have earnestly tried to bring that about, I think with some success, at all events in Ontario and a little further west. The right way is for the Provincial Governments to reduce the judiciary until every judge will have a day's work every day of the year except during a proper holiday. I do not think they have done that in Ontario, but they have gone a long way towards doing it. Very shortly we shall have twenty-five fewer judges in Ontario,-there are a great many who would not weep if the figure were larger. I think that Saskatchewan might very well take a pattern from Ontario in this regard. There are now seventeen county court judges in Saskatchewan; there will be eighteen when this legislation passes. It would take a long time to convince me that Saskatchewan could nbt so distribute its district court judiciary as to provide that every member of the Bench would have his time fully occupied the year round, save during a reasonable holiday period. That is what the judges themselves would like, and that is common sense. But the outcome of the application of the principle that is embedded in our constitution, that the province creates the Bench and creates the vacancies, leaving it to the Dominion to fill them and to pay the salaries, is a surplus of vacancies, a multitude of judges, inadequate salaries, and an improper distribution of judicial burdens.
I assume the minister does not approve of what has already been done in the singling out of the four municipalities which I have mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is done away with by these resolutions; the salary of every county court or district court judge is made $4,000, no matter where he is. I do not know whether Ontario provides differently so far as the busier judges in Toronto and other large places are concerned, but the Dominion pays exactly the same to all.

I am very much impressed by what my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island has said with regard to the judiciary of his province being not fairly treated, having regard to the treatment accorded to the judiciary in other provinces. I am not so well informed with regard to the claims of Quebec, but the arguments made with regard to the treatment of -.he judiciary of that province seem to be strong as well. I suggest that the minister let this whole matter stand for the .time being. I know that that suggestion will not be very popular among the judiciary of my province, but I feel that we are going a long way when we ask Parliament to vote about $250,000 a year for the purpose of increasing the salaries of judges throughout Canada. The Government are increasing

the salaries of officials who are already fairly well paid and not paying sufficient attention to civil servants who receive lesser salaries than they should receive, having regard to the responsibilities of their positions. In New Brunswick there are seven judges of the Superior Court. Two chief justices are receiving $7,000 a year. On& of the puisne judges is judge of the Divorce Court, for which he receives an extra $1,000 a year, bringing his salary up to $7,000. Another of the puisne judges is judge of the Admiralty Court, and as such receives an extra $1,000 a year, which brings him also up to $7,000. Under this Bill, therefore, four members of the bench will get $8,000 a year and three will get $7,000 a year. The only justification for increasing these salaries at this time would be an inability to induce good lawyers or barristers to give up their practice and accept judgeships. I do not know what the experience has been in the other provinces, but I am glad to say that in New Brunswick we have been able to induce barristers of the highest standing to leave their profession and don the ermine; the judiciary of our province stands second to none in the Dominion. Three judges, men of very high standing, have been appointed in New Brunswick during the last two years. When a judge is appointed he knows what salary he is to receive; we are now asking him to accept a. bonus of $1,000 which he did not expect. I doubt very much whether these gentlemen have asked the Government to pay them this amount. I know of men in New Brunswick who hold responsible positions in the Civil Service, who are subject to the same high cost of living as the judges are, and who have to subsist on only $1,200 a year.
Yet we to-night are asked to hand over $1,000 extra to every one of these judges, or an amount practically equal to the salaries of many civil servants holding responsible positions, who have families to support just as the judges have. I have been impressed with this in thinking over the matter, because it is with some hesitation I make this protest, as I know the judges of my province, having practised with them and before them. Nevertheless, I doubt very much whether it is the duty of Parliament at this time to make this additional expenditure in order to benefit gentlemen who are now occupying positions as judges. The President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), the other night, almost with tears in his eyes, pointed out how the committee, who had been investigating the question of pensions for the widows and orphans of soldiers who had gone overseas and sacrificed their lives

in the defence of the country, had been magnanimous enough to give the widow with a family from $800 to $1,000 per annum. That means that she must rear and educate her children on less' than the amount by which we are bonusing the judges. Is it fair to those people, to the lower-paid civil servants, to us all, that we should at this time increase our expenditure to the extent of $250,000 in order to give this extra allowance to the members of our judiciary? At an opportune time, when our finances are in better shape, and when we are in a position to give to ordinary civil servants a reasonable salary as well, I shall have no protest to make, but I take the responsibility here of protesting against this increase, although I know that some of the judges in my province may not thank me for my action. Nevertheless, I believe a number of the members of the judiciary of New Brunswick, if the question were put to them fairly and squarely: Do you think, under present conditions, you should be given this increase?-would say: We are quite satisfied at the present time with what we have; we believe to-day a little economy should be practised. I know some of them would take that position, because I have talked with them. Until we are able to give our lower-paid civil servants a -little better salary to enable them to maintain their families in reasonable comfort, I feel that the Government would not be well advised at the present time in incurring this extra expenditure.

I have very little to add to what I said when this matter was before the committee on a previous occasion, except to express again my deep regret and sense of disappointment that so great an inequality is to continue to exist, and to be aggravated beyond what it was, between the salaries received by the judges of the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island and those received by judges occupying similar positions in other provinces of -Canada. The difference between the Chief Justice and the puisne judges respectively with regard to similar judges in the other provinces is $1,500, and that is a great inequality. It has been said already that the material of which judges are made in Prince Edward Island is quite as good as that from which judges are made in any other part of Canada. Evidence of this can be found from the positions which members of the Prince Edward Island bar have taken in the judiciary, not only of Prince Edward Island, but of other parts of the country and in the fact that the present Chief Justice of the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Supreme Court of Canada is a member of the Prince Edward Island bar.
Just one other point. The increase in the salaries of county court judges is equalized throughout Canada; their salaries are increased for Prince Edward Island as well as for every other province and are made equal. If the argument put forward by the Acting Minister of Justice that the duties are, perhaps, not so onerous in Prince Edward Island, holds good as regards judges of the Supreme Court, I am sure it will be doubly true as regards judges of the county court in that province. I do not think their labours are extremely onerous, and it would look as if judges of the Supreme Court were penalized in comparison with judges of the county court. I just wish to register my sense of disappointment and regret that this great inequality, and what I regard as an injustice to judges of the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island, should be allowed to exist.	.

The minister stated that per head the administration of justice was higher in Prince Edward Island than in the other provinces. We cannot help that, and there is no argument in that to retain our judges at lower salaries. The judge is not the whole administration of justice. In order to have justice administered and properly guarded in Prince Edward Island, we must have penitentiaries and so forth, -and from what I know there are not many criminals from Prince Edward Island kept in penitentiaries. Confederation was entered into by certain provinces in 1867, and we had our doubts then whether we would get fair treatment on account of our being a small province. Every time when we come up here and ask for anything in this Parliament, the reply is made: Oh, Prince Edward Island costs so much. We never asked to be permitted to enter Confederation; you came down there and plenipotentiaries were sent from Great Britain. We came in Confederation in 1873, or six years later, and at that time we were free of debt. Moreover, we handed over a railway that cost Prince Edward Island $3,400,000, which means that we have been penalized to tne extent of $170,000 per year,seeing t-hatwe must contribute our share in respect of railways built elsewhere in Canada. Yet we are told if we ask for anything, that Prince Edward Island costs so much. The other day I went home and I found an arbitrary charge of $5 per ton on freight going over the ferry. Why is there this discrimination? When I ask the minister the reason, he cannot tell me why, and
his deputy cannot tell me why. I, for one, am not going to put up with this, and I tell the minister that I will follow this thing up, now that I have got hold of it, and if we do not get fair play and if he does not consent to give these judges an increase of $1,000, we shall oppose the resolution.
Come over to this side oi the House.

I am not asking, in suggesting this increese of $1,000, that the salary of our Chief Justice should be as high as that of the Chief Justice of the neighbouring province. Our Chief Justice will still have $1,000 less, and it is only fair for the minister to think the matter over to-morrow morning, and bring down an amendment to the resolution so as to give our Supreme Court judges an increase of $1,000 like the other judges, and then I shall be satisfied. It cannot be regarded as anything less than a downright discrimination against our province. We are a small province with only four representatives although we ought to have six, but we are going to fight for our rights.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I cannot agree with
my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) in opposition to this resolution, because I have for a long time been asking for these increases. I suggested to the minister at the time that he should make the salaries of the county court judges, $5,000. I regret that'he did not adopt that suggestion. We gave our deputy ministers $6,000, and I would be sorry to think that the position of the judge of a county court was not of equal importance to that of a deputy minister. However, it is a -fair advance, and I am grateful to the minister for what he has done, and will express the hope that later on when the finances are better a still further advance will be made to those gentlemen who are serving the country so well. When we were discussing this subject some weeks ago I suggested to the minister that when the increases were made in 1906 we forgot the Supreme Court of Canada, and it looks as if we are forgetting. it again. I suppose those judges will expect increases as well as the others. I am particularly thankful to the minister that he has put Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, British Columbia and other provinces exactly upon the same footing as Quebec and Ontario. I fully agree with my friend from Prince Edward Island in his complaint.' It requires the same qualifications to be Chief Justice of Prince Edward Island as it does

to be Chief Justice of Nova Scotia. He must be conversant with the criminal law so that when a man is on trial for his life he may be able properly to instruct the jury. Criminal law is the same all over the country and the same knowledge is called for in Prince Edward Island as in any other part of Canada. It does not matter that the province is small. Law is a science and the men who administer it must have scientific knowledge. Those of us who are lawyers are proud of the science, and we feel that men who are in responsible positions on the bench should be recognized as discharging highly important duties. I think it would be splendid courage-if I may use that term-for the minister to put the little province of Prince Edward Island, with only three judges, in	exactly	the same position as any other province so that their judges and chief justice would hold his head just as high as any other puisne judge or chief justice in any other part of Canada. It is only a small matter, and we could say with pride that while Prince Edward Island was small we treated it exactly like the others. If we cross the border we will find in Rhode Island, which is very small in area compared with Prince Edward Island, the judges and senators there, and everything else for that matter, on the same footing as in the state of New York. Because we have a little province such as Prince Edward Island is no reason why we should allow the salaries of the judges there to be less than in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or elsewhere. I have already brought to' the notice of the minister the fact that the county court judge in Winnipeg, which is one of the metropolitan cities of Canada, wrote me that he was not getting the $500 which was paid to the judge in St. John and the judge at Halifax. I do not know whether the minister forgot that distinction or not. I am very much obliged to the minister for what he has [DOT] done. I must add my word of protest to that of my friends from Quebec who think the bench there is not fairly treated, and I trust that an opportunity will be given before long to have 'these matters dealt with again when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), who has more extensive knowledge of conditions in that province, is here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
One would actually think, listening to the tone of certain hon. members to-night, that I was the first offender in the way of drawing a distinction

between the salaries of judges in Prince Edward Island and those in other parts of Canada. I know of no time when it has not been drawn, I know of no country in the world where the same principle is not recognized. That is a pretty sweeping statement, but it applies throughout the British Empire. Where the duties and the responsibilities are less,, though the profession may be the same, the remuneration is less. There is nothing new in this, and there is no accentuation of anything that has hitherto prevailed. The same thing appertains in Canada in relation to other duties, and it appertains in the United States in the judiciary throughout the length and breadth of the country. Does any one think for a moment that there are as many important cases, or even a reasonable fraction of as many as important cases that come before, and have to be decided by, the high court judge in Prince Edward Island as by the high court judge in Ontario? No, one in his sane senses would suggest it. As regards .the salaries of the county court judge in St. John and the county court judge in Westmorland, I would ask the hon. member, who thinks there should be a readjustment, is not the science of law the same in St. John as in Westmorland?
Why does he want it?-because the duties are somewhat more onerous in St. John. That is correct but the right way to remedy that is by a redistribution of the duties rather than by a differenee~in the salaries. If we could remedy it in Prince Edward Island in the same way I would be very glad indeed, but we cannot remedy it in the same way. Consequently, we simply try to be fair and reasonable, and I am not going to be diverted from that course by threatening,s of reprisal or of slaughter no matter in what language pronounced.

Under the rule that the
minister has laid down, that where the responsibility is greater the salary is greater, the judges in Quebec, and particularly in Montreal should have very much larger salaries than the judges in any other part of Canada, because on the island of Montreal we have ten per cent of the entire population of Canada and questions of the most important and intricate character come before these courts of law. It is a large metropolitan centre, and it does seem to me that the salaries that our judges are getting are not at all in proportion to the work they are performing. I was criticised, I understand, a day or two ago, for a certain reference that I made to some of our judges. Notwithstanding that I want

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: to say that I consider that the judges in Montreal particularly are very much underpaid. How is it possible for a High Court judge in a large centre like Montreal to live on the paltry salary of $7,000 a year where the dollar has shrunk in the last four or five years to forty per cent of its former value? Yet, we expect that judges can keep up their positions socially and otherwise on the paltry sum of $7,000 a year. How can it be expected that we can get the best class of men to ascend the bench and leave a lucrative practice for $7,000? It is impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) says it is cheaper to live in Montreal on account of the departmental stores and bargain sales.

My hon. friend from Three Rivers must have been reading the advertisements in the daily newspapers in regard to department stores, but if he came to live in Montreal he would probably change his tune. Montreal is one of the dearest places in Canada to live in to-day, and if we want to keep up the tone of our bench, or to see to it that we have on the bench men of the high type that we have had in the past, it certainly behooves the Government to take up this question and see that the judges get a living wage. An ordinary river pilot to-day gets as .much as a Superior Court judge. A travelling salesman gets more than a judge does, and a designer in a clothing factory gets a very much larger salary than a judge. The Government increase salaries in the Civil Service; in fact, salaries are increased all along the line except in the case of the judiciary. I am even in favour of increasing the salaries of the members of the Government. I do not see1 how they can live on what they are getting. If we want to obtain the services of the best people we must pay for them, and the sooner the Government recognize that the better it will be for the country.

As I said a few moments ago, I would like to see the provisions contained in this resolution incorporated in a Bill and passed. In 1905 when the judges' salaries were increased there was a provision, put into the Act that judges should not do any outside work. That provision has only been partially observed. Some judges are appointed on commissions and get large fees outside of their salaries for acting on these commissions. They are nearly always the same judges who get these appointments. There is one in Ontario who is appointed for any work that is required in that province. In Quebec also, it is
nearly always the same judge who is appointed by this Government to act on a commission. They get large fees and they get their salaries besides. It is not fair, because their judicial work suffers in the meantime. If they are employed for any length of time on commissions they cannot perform their judicial duties satisfactorily.
I would like to see the provision adopted by the Senate put into this Bill that all the fees they receive for acting on commissions or on any other tribunals, outside of their judicial work, shall be deducted from their salaries.

I want to add another word to what I said a few days ago when these resolutions were before the House. I stated then quite clearly my objections to the increases that were going to be given by the Acting Minister of Justice to the judges of the Supreme Cburt of Prince Edward Island, and I am of the same opinion now, I have not changed my opinion in any way since the resolution was up before. I took the ground that there should be no distinction between the salaries paid to the Supreme Court judges in Prince Edward Island and the salaries paid to judges in other provinces. The minister has told us that the object of this resolution is to equalize the salaries of the Supreme Court judges in all the provinces of Canada except Prince Edward Island, and it is doing so. While I believe that to be right, I would agree with my corepresentative who says, that if the minister would consent to reconsider his position and give the straight, or proportionate, increase to the Supreme Court judges of Prince Edward Island that he has given to the Supreme Court judges of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, thus adding $1,000 per year to their present salaries, it would be better than 'the increase which is now proposed. I cannot see upon what ground the minister bases the increase that he is giving to the Supreme Court judges of Prince Edward Island. It is not fair to put the cost of the administration of justice on a per capita basis in Prince Edward Island. It was known when we entered Confederation that the administration of justice could not be carried on as cheaply per capita in Prince Edward Island as it could be in the upper provinces of Canada. We know quite well that when the Fathers of Confederation accepted the terms upon which we entered the Confederation in 1873 and under which they agreed to pay the salaries of the Supreme Court judges, they knew quite well

that they could not be met as cheaply per capita as in the larger provinces of 'Canada, and it is not fair to the minister to cite that as a reason why these salaries should not be further increased. It has almost become a habit of this Government to discriminate against Prince Edward Island. I do not know that it would be in order to mention it but we may have an opportunity before long of discussing the reclassification of the Civil Service which has been brought down and which has shown a similar discrimination as against the Outside Service in Prince Edward Island. This discrimination has spread from one department to another, and it is high time that it should cease and that the Government should recognize that Prince Edward Island is a province having status equal to that of any other province in Confederation. The minister tells us that he is making no distinction in salaries as against Prince Edward Island, that the distinction has existed. But I think the minister must admit that he is drawing a distinction in the increases of salaries that he is providing for in this proposed resolution. I stated the other day that the increases were about one-half, on a percentage basis, those given to the judges of the other Maritime Provinces. That I do not consider fair.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What about Ontario and Quebec?

The minister showed that we were $500 nearer Ontario in the matter of salaries, but if he would apply the same reasoning to the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island would come $1,000 nearer to Ontario. Is it fair that the salaries of the judges in those provinces should be raised $1,000 and the judges' salaries in Prince Edward Island only increased by $500 ? I do not see how the minister can synchronize these two sets of conditions by the legislation which he proposes. Another point emphasized by the minister is that on account of less work and less responsibility there should be less pay. But when we see that the judges of our Supreme Court are not allowed to engage in other activities, such, for example, as becoming directors or managers of industrial enterprises, but must confine themselves strictly to their judicial duties, we cannot measure their pay according to the work they do. We must uphold the dignity of the judges of the Supreme Court, whose time is entirely devoted to the discharge of their judicial duties. It is, therefore, hardly 
fair to say that on the ground of performing less work or assuming less responsibility they should receive less salary. I think the minister should reconsider his decision in regard to the salaries of the Supreme Court judges in Prince Edward Island and grant to them the same increases which he has given in the case of the judges in the other Maritime Provinces. While that would to some extent meet the case, it would not be entirely satisfactory, as there would still be a discrimination as between the salaries paid to the judges of Prince Edward Island and those paid to the judges in the other provinces of Canada.
Resolutions reported, read the first and second time, and concurred in.
Hon. Mr. Meighen moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 177, to amend the Judges Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think it is now about time for the House to adjourn.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Meighen, the House adjourned at 12.20 a.m.
Wednesday, July 2nd, 1919.
